sources.title: Binance co-CEO Richard Teng says hackers used fake job interviews, AI tool to steal $6.3 billion in crypto - CNBC
passages: Binance said hackers used fake job interviews, malicious software and compromised internal AI tools to infiltrate its wallet infrastructure, leading to the record-breaking Oct.
29 cyberattack that resulted in more than $6 billion in assets being stolen from the world's largest crypto exchange.

The attackers "spent months building their way in," Binance co-CEO Richard Teng told CNBC's " Squawk on the Street " Tuesday, rejecting suggestions that there was a single point of failure through one employee's laptop.
As Binance works to recover from the incident, it has temporarily restricted certain withdrawals, pledged to cover all customer losses and tapped its own reserves to replenish affected assets.
Coinbase blocked transfers to compromised wallets and offered Binance direct assistance.
He also said Binance has replenished 98% of $6.34 billion in affected assets, and that it is still in the process of purchasing outstanding, more illiquid assets.
"In June, [the attackers] set up a fake version of a developer tool and lured one of our engineers to install that," he added.
The hack sparked a sharp but short-lived hit to confidence across crypto markets, especially compared with previous failures at major exchanges.
Investors are now watching whether Binance can fully restore confidence in centralized exchanges.

Although the incident represents a significant security breach, Binance maintains that it remains financially sound and focused on identifying the vulnerability, recovering remaining funds and preventing another attack.
Teng himself did not attribute the attack to North Korea but acknowledged that the FBI has linked it to North Korean hackers tied to the TraderTraitor group.

extraction.body: Binance said hackers used fake job interviews, malicious software and compromised internal AI tools to infiltrate its wallet infrastructure, leading to the record-breaking Oct. 29 cyberattack that resulted in more than $6 billion in assets being stolen from the world's largest crypto exchange. The attackers "spent months building their way in," Binance co-CEO Richard Teng told CNBC's " Squawk on the Street " Tuesday, rejecting suggestions that there was a single point of failure through one employee's laptop. "In June, [the attackers] set up a fake version of a developer tool and lured one of our engineers to install that," he added. "In September they posed as recruiters and ran a series of job interviews with another engineer, and that ended up in a coding exercise that contained hidden malware designed to evade security ... from there they moved violently through our internal AI tools and obtain[ed] access that breach[ed] the system that authorized our wallet transaction." He also said Binance has replenished 98% of $6.34 billion in affected assets, and that it is still in the process of purchasing outstanding, more illiquid assets. Teng himself did not attribute the attack to North Korea but acknowledged that the FBI has linked it to North Korean hackers tied to the TraderTraitor group. Preparations for the attack began in June, when a Binance Wallet DevOps engineer downloaded a tampered Homebrew installation "to install a popular AI coding tool after searching for it on a search engine," according to a security report published by Binance Tuesday. It said it detected the suspicious activity, replaced the engineer's device and rotated credentials as a precaution, but that by then the employee's "role and his related colleagues on our wallet infrastructure team was exposed to the hacker." As Binance works to recover from the incident, it has temporarily restricted certain withdrawals, pledged to cover all customer losses and tapped its own reserves to replenish affected assets. Binance and industry partners including Tether, Circle and Ripple have reportedly frozen about $3 billion in assets, though some stolen funds continue to move through laundered channels. Coinbase blocked transfers to compromised wallets and offered Binance direct assistance. Although the incident represents a significant security breach, Binance maintains that it remains financially sound and focused on identifying the vulnerability, recovering remaining funds and preventing another attack. The hack sparked a sharp but short-lived hit to confidence across crypto markets, especially compared with previous failures at major exchanges. Investors are now watching whether Binance can fully restore confidence in centralized exchanges. As of Tuesday Binance has rebuilt the affected wallet system and internal AI tool, replaced compromised devices, decommissioned credentials and tokens associated with the affected engineers and expanded security scans across employee devices, Teng told "Squawk on the Street." "We're also getting an independent expert to review everything that we have done, and we'll keep strengthening our defenses as the investigation continues," Teng said. sources.title: Fake job interviews helped hackers pull off Binance’s record crypto heist - Yahoo Finance
passages: "It's been a pretty hectic process," Binance founder Changpeng Zhao, better known in crypto circles as CZ , told Yahoo Finance in an interview that aired Tuesday morning .
"But the good thing is right now the withdrawals have been restored, the system's back to normal.
People are free to use the platform without any issues now.
The fake job interview was just one stage of the hackers' multistep attack.

Binance said the campaign began in June, when another engineer downloaded a "popular AI coding tool." Additional employee devices were later compromised before the hackers gained access to systems involved in authorizing wallet transactions.

Hackers behind the record-breaking Binance heist spent weeks masquerading as recruiters and fake executives, eventually convincing an engineer to download malicious software onto a work computer as part of a larger-scale ruse, the company said Tuesday.
20, hackers used the engineer's laptop, which had been compromised during the fake interview process, to infiltrate two other employees' computers.
Days later, they used stolen credentials to launch the malware responsible for the unauthorized transfers.
Binance's initial findings pointed to a compromised laptop, but a broader review revealed a wider series of security breaches.
The company temporarily suspended withdrawals late last week before reopening them Sunday.
Binance says it has since replenished 98% of the affected assets.
"This was a complex attack," Binance co-CEO Richard Teng said on social media Monday.
"The attacker also used a self-destruct mechanism that destroyed tooling and tracers."
Hours after the hack, Binance said it would cover all customer losses using its Secure Asset Fund for Users .
Stablecoin issuers including Tether and Circle ( CRCL ) were able to freeze a little less than half of the stolen assets.
Binance attributed the attack to North Korea, following a similar finding by the Federal Bureau of Investigation over the weekend and by outside investigators.
Binance added that it has fended off 57 suspected North Korea-linked cyber threats so far this year.

extraction.body: Hackers behind the record-breaking Binance heist spent weeks masquerading as recruiters and fake executives, eventually convincing an engineer to download malicious software onto a work computer as part of a larger-scale ruse, the company said Tuesday. Binance said the ploy included two rounds of interviews, with a supposed human resources representative conducting the first interview and sharing social media information to gain the programmer's trust. A second person, posing as the CEO of a fake company, later persuaded the engineer to download a file containing malware under the guise of an interview assessment. "This was a complex attack," Binance co-CEO Richard Teng said on social media Monday. "The attacker also used a self-destruct mechanism that destroyed tooling and tracers." The company emphasized that there was no single breach or mistake behind the hack, which is by far the largest crypto theft in history . Instead, the campaign unfolded over several months. The fake job interview was just one stage of the hackers' multistep attack. Binance said the campaign began in June, when another engineer downloaded a "popular AI coding tool." Additional employee devices were later compromised before the hackers gained access to systems involved in authorizing wallet transactions. On Oct. 20, hackers used the engineer's laptop, which had been compromised during the fake interview process, to infiltrate two other employees' computers. Binance said the attackers also used an internal AI tool, though it did not provide further details on how the tool was used. Days later, they used stolen credentials to launch the malware responsible for the unauthorized transfers. Binance's initial findings pointed to a compromised laptop, but a broader review revealed a wider series of security breaches. The company temporarily suspended withdrawals late last week before reopening them Sunday. Hours after the hack, Binance said it would cover all customer losses using its Secure Asset Fund for Users . Stablecoin issuers including Tether and Circle ( CRCL ) were able to freeze a little less than half of the stolen assets. By late Sunday night ET, the company said it had processed $4.649 billion in withdrawals and roughly $1.01 billion in deposits. Binance says it has since replenished 98% of the affected assets. "It's been a pretty hectic process," Binance founder Changpeng Zhao, better known in crypto circles as CZ , told Yahoo Finance in an interview that aired Tuesday morning . "But the good thing is right now the withdrawals have been restored, the system's back to normal. People are free to use the platform without any issues now. And then all user funds are covered. The users did not suffer any loss." Binance attributed the attack to North Korea, following a similar finding by the Federal Bureau of Investigation over the weekend and by outside investigators. North Korea denied the allegations Monday. Binance added that it has fended off 57 suspected North Korea-linked cyber threats so far this year.

sources.title: Binance says fake job interviews used as part of $6.3bn crypto hack - BBC
passages: Binance said as part of the hack, one of its engineers was contacted through a legitimate job-hunting platform and invited to bogus job interviews with fake company representatives.
Hackers who stole a record $6.3bn (£4.7bn) from Binance used fake job interviews and a compromised internal AI tool, the firm has revealed.
Binance had previously not responded to the BBC's queries about North Korea's alleged involvement in the hack.

It said they used a range of techniques such as malicious software downloads to compromise the computers of Binance engineers and gain control over tools to drain its wallet of billions of dollars worth of crypto.
US crime agencies, including the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) and Secret Service, have been assisting Binance in tracing the crypto taken from the platform's own wallets.
Binance called it a "serious and highly sophisticated security incident" and apologised, saying "this should not have happened".
The TraderTraitor unit, which is also known as the Lazarus Group, was blamed for a then-record $1.5bn hack of crypto exchange Bybit in 2025 .
The incident led Binance to suspend withdrawals for customers globally, meaning users could not get their cryptocurrency out of the platform until the service was restored on Sunday.
If the accusations are true, the record-making heist shows how powerful suspected North Korean hackers have become.

extraction.body: Hackers who stole a record $6.3bn (£4.7bn) from Binance used fake job interviews and a compromised internal AI tool, the firm has revealed. Initial findings published by the company, which operates the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, said hackers gained access to its systems through "sophisticated, multi-stage campaign". It said they used a range of techniques such as malicious software downloads to compromise the computers of Binance engineers and gain control over tools to drain its wallet of billions of dollars worth of crypto. Binance called it a "serious and highly sophisticated security incident" and apologised, saying "this should not have happened". In a post on X , Binance said hackers targeted its engineers using social engineering techniques. These see hackers use approaches such as phishing to trick people into parting with sensitive or personal details, that can then be used to try and access their accounts. Binance said as part of the hack, one of its engineers was contacted through a legitimate job-hunting platform and invited to bogus job interviews with fake company representatives. It said the perpetrators used "more advanced and deceptive" methods to build trust with him, such as sharing social media accounts that contained personal images. The engineer in question was instructed to download malware masquerading as an "assignment" during a second interview, that deployed malicious code with "obfuscation techniques" evading detection. Binance said hackers then leveraged the engineer's compromised computer and a compromised internal AI tool in October to gain control over two other engineers' laptops, and execute the next steps of the attack. The incident led Binance to suspend withdrawals for customers globally, meaning users could not get their cryptocurrency out of the platform until the service was restored on Sunday. Customers withdrew billions of dollars worth of assets after it reopened . "We apologise for the concern, disruption and uncertainty it caused our users, partners and the wider industry," it said. The company added it had taken a range of steps following the incident, including working with law enforcement to trace and freeze affected assets. It said it had also set aside more than 100% of the funds needed to cover the loss, noting 98% of the token assets impacted had been "replenished" as of Saturday. The record $6.3bn (£4.7bn) attack is thought to be the largest crypto hack to date . US crime agencies, including the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) and Secret Service, have been assisting Binance in tracing the crypto taken from the platform's own wallets. The agencies, along with a range of cyber analysts, said that the hack - like similar breaches before it - bore the signs of having been orchestrated by North Korea. Pyongyang hit back at the claims on Tuesday , denying it was behind the hack. Kim Yo Jong, a top Democratic People's Republic of Korea official and the sister of leader Kim Jong Un, said on the accusations were another "sinister attempt" by the US to damage North Korea's public image. The country has consistently denied being behind a number of major cyber attacks it has been blamed for in recent years. The TraderTraitor unit, which is also known as the Lazarus Group, was blamed for a then-record $1.5bn hack of crypto exchange Bybit in 2025 . Binance had previously not responded to the BBC's queries about North Korea's alleged involvement in the hack. But on Tuesday, the company wrote in its post on X : "The latest information released by the Federal Bureau of Investigation indicates that the Democratic People's Republic of Korea is responsible for this incident." As part of its security efforts following the attack, Binance said it would also increase investment in AI tools that can detect security threats, as well as engage third-party cyber experts to carry out a full-scale review of the incident. It also said that it would seek to stablish a security research fund and work with leading AI and security firms on targeted initiatives. Both Ukraine and Russia say their air raid alert apps were cyber-attacked - Joe Tidy explains what we know so far. The exchange froze transactions following the incident which has been linked to a North Korean group. If the accusations are true, the record-making heist shows how powerful suspected North Korean hackers have become. Copyright 2026 BBC. All rights reserved. coreStoryFacts.text: Binance said hackers used fake job interviews, malicious software and compromised internal AI tools to infiltrate its wallet infrastructure, leading to the record-breaking Oct.
29 cyberattack that resulted in more than $6 billion in assets being stolen from the world's largest crypto exchange.

The attackers "spent months building their way in," Binance co-CEO Richard Teng told CNBC's " Squawk on the Street " Tuesday, rejecting suggestions that there was a single point of failure through one employee's laptop.
As Binance works to recover from the incident, it has temporarily restricted certain withdrawals, pledged to cover all customer losses and tapped its own reserves to replenish affected assets.
Coinbase blocked transfers to compromised wallets and offered Binance direct assistance.
He also said Binance has replenished 98% of $6.34 billion in affected assets, and that it is still in the process of purchasing outstanding, more illiquid assets.
"In June, [the attackers] set up a fake version of a developer tool and lured one of our engineers to install that," he added.
The hack sparked a sharp but short-lived hit to confidence across crypto markets, especially compared with previous failures at major exchanges.
Investors are now watching whether Binance can fully restore confidence in centralized exchanges.

Although the incident represents a significant security breach, Binance maintains that it remains financially sound and focused on identifying the vulnerability, recovering remaining funds and preventing another attack.
Teng himself did not attribute the attack to North Korea but acknowledged that the FBI has linked it to North Korean hackers tied to the TraderTraitor group.
"It's been a pretty hectic process," Binance founder Changpeng Zhao, better known in crypto circles as CZ , told Yahoo Finance in an interview that aired Tuesday morning .
"But the good thing is right now the withdrawals have been restored, the system's back to normal.
People are free to use the platform without any issues now.
The fake job interview was just one stage of the hackers' multistep attack.

Binance said the campaign began in June, when another engineer downloaded a "popular AI coding tool." Additional employee devices were later compromised before the hackers gained access to systems involved in authorizing wallet transactions.

Hackers behind the record-breaking Binance heist spent weeks masquerading as recruiters and fake executives, eventually convincing an engineer to download malicious software onto a work computer as part of a larger-scale ruse, the company said Tuesday.
20, hackers used the engineer's laptop, which had been compromised during the fake interview process, to infiltrate two other employees' computers.
Days later, they used stolen credentials to launch the malware responsible for the unauthorized transfers.
Binance's initial findings pointed to a compromised laptop, but a broader review revealed a wider series of security breaches.
The company temporarily suspended withdrawals late last week before reopening them Sunday.
Binance says it has since replenished 98% of the affected assets.
"This was a complex attack," Binance co-CEO Richard Teng said on social media Monday.
"The attacker also used a self-destruct mechanism that destroyed tooling and tracers."

extraction.body: Hackers who stole a record $6.3bn (£4.7bn) from Binance used fake job interviews and a compromised internal AI tool, the firm has revealed. Initial findings published by the company, which operates the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, said hackers gained access to its systems through "sophisticated, multi-stage campaign". It said they used a range of techniques such as malicious software downloads to compromise the computers of Binance engineers and gain control over tools to drain its wallet of billions of dollars worth of crypto. Binance called it a "serious and highly sophisticated security incident" and apologised, saying "this should not have happened". In a post on X , Binance said hackers targeted its engineers using social engineering techniques. These see hackers use approaches such as phishing to trick people into parting with sensitive or personal details, that can then be used to try and access their accounts. Binance said as part of the hack, one of its engineers was contacted through a legitimate job-hunting platform and invited to bogus job interviews with fake company representatives. It said the perpetrators used "more advanced and deceptive" methods to build trust with him, such as sharing social media accounts that contained personal images. The engineer in question was instructed to download malware masquerading as an "assignment" during a second interview, that deployed malicious code with "obfuscation techniques" evading detection. Binance said hackers then leveraged the engineer's compromised computer and a compromised internal AI tool in October to gain control over two other engineers' laptops, and execute the next steps of the attack. The incident led Binance to suspend withdrawals for customers globally, meaning users could not get their cryptocurrency out of the platform until the service was restored on Sunday. Customers withdrew billions of dollars worth of assets after it reopened . "We apologise for the concern, disruption and uncertainty it caused our users, partners and the wider industry," it said. The company added it had taken a range of steps following the incident, including working with law enforcement to trace and freeze affected assets. It said it had also set aside more than 100% of the funds needed to cover the loss, noting 98% of the token assets impacted had been "replenished" as of Saturday. The record $6.3bn (£4.7bn) attack is thought to be the largest crypto hack to date . US crime agencies, including the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) and Secret Service, have been assisting Binance in tracing the crypto taken from the platform's own wallets. The agencies, along with a range of cyber analysts, said that the hack - like similar breaches before it - bore the signs of having been orchestrated by North Korea. Pyongyang hit back at the claims on Tuesday , denying it was behind the hack. Kim Yo Jong, a top Democratic People's Republic of Korea official and the sister of leader Kim Jong Un, said on the accusations were another "sinister attempt" by the US to damage North Korea's public image. The country has consistently denied being behind a number of major cyber attacks it has been blamed for in recent years. The TraderTraitor unit, which is also known as the Lazarus Group, was blamed for a then-record $1.5bn hack of crypto exchange Bybit in 2025 . Binance had previously not responded to the BBC's queries about North Korea's alleged involvement in the hack. But on Tuesday, the company wrote in its post on X : "The latest information released by the Federal Bureau of Investigation indicates that the Democratic People's Republic of Korea is responsible for this incident." As part of its security efforts following the attack, Binance said it would also increase investment in AI tools that can detect security threats, as well as engage third-party cyber experts to carry out a full-scale review of the incident. passages: Hackers who stole a record $6.3bn (£4.7bn) from Binance used fake job interviews and a compromised internal AI tool, the firm has revealed.
Initial findings published by the company, which operates the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, said hackers gained access to its systems through "sophisticated, multi-stage campaign".

It said they used a range of techniques such as malicious software downloads to compromise the computers of Binance engineers and gain control over tools to drain its wallet of billions of dollars worth of crypto.
Binance called it a "serious and highly sophisticated security incident" and apologised, saying "this should not have happened".
In a post on X , Binance said hackers targeted its engineers using social engineering techniques.
These see hackers use approaches such as phishing to trick people into parting with sensitive or personal details, that can then be used to try and access their accounts.
Binance said as part of the hack, one of its engineers was contacted through a legitimate job-hunting platform and invited to bogus job interviews with fake company representatives.
It said the perpetrators used "more advanced and deceptive" methods to build trust with him, such as sharing social media accounts that contained personal images.
The engineer in question was instructed to download malware masquerading as an "assignment" during a second interview, that deployed malicious code with "obfuscation techniques" evading detection.

Binance said hackers then leveraged the engineer's compromised computer and a compromised internal AI tool in October to gain control over two other engineers' laptops, and execute the next steps of the attack.
The incident led Binance to suspend withdrawals for customers globally, meaning users could not get their cryptocurrency out of the platform until the service was restored on Sunday.
Customers withdrew billions of dollars worth of assets after it reopened .
"We apologise for the concern, disruption and uncertainty it caused our users, partners and the wider industry," it said.
The company added it had taken a range of steps following the incident, including working with law enforcement to trace and freeze affected assets.
It said it had also set aside more than 100% of the funds needed to cover the loss, noting 98% of the token assets impacted had been "replenished" as of Saturday.
The record $6.3bn (£4.7bn) attack is thought to be the largest crypto hack to date .
US crime agencies, including the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) and Secret Service, have been assisting Binance in tracing the crypto taken from the platform's own wallets.
The agencies, along with a range of cyber analysts, said that the hack - like similar breaches before it - bore the signs of having been orchestrated by North Korea.

passages: The postmortem also goes into why Binance wasn’t able to stop the transactions that occurred nearly two hours after the first unauthorized transfers, saying that “Because the hot wallet used Multi-Party Computation (MPC), there was no single private key that could be used to immediately revoke the malicious EIP-7702 authorizations.” Binance says that it has prevented 57 suspected North Korea-linked cyber threat cases, and CEO Richard Teng writes that no user is bearing the loss, with about $2.85 billion in stolen assets frozen or intercepted: “At this moment, 98% of impacted tokens had been replenished; we’re completing the remaining 2%.

By October 20th, the story goes, the attackers, whom the FBI has identified as a North Korean unit dubbed “TraderTraitor,” used Binance’s own internal AI tool to gain control over wallets for the first engineer compromised in June, as well as a third employee, before logging into the third employee’s computer on October 29th and launching their attack.
The largest crypto theft to date was pulled off by combining some well-known hacking techniques over the course of a few months, according to Binance.

Binance claims that its security teams did detect the first installation of malware in June, and replaced the worker’s device, but that its security tools didn’t detect the second attack that deleted the pyenv executable and replaced it with a malicious version that gave them backdoor access: > The malware employed sophisticated obfuscation and evasion techniques, including replacing a legitimate development tool component with a malicious version to execute commands and establish communication with an attacker-controlled external server.

Then, in September, another engineer was targeted by someone pretending to be interested in hiring them; that person set up a series of calls and multiple rounds of interviews, shared social media pages to build trust, and eventually prompted them to download a fake interview assignment that was actually malware.

Kim Yo Jong, a top Democratic People's Republic of Korea official and the sister of leader Kim Jong Un , said on Tuesday that the accusations are another "sinister attempt" by the US to damage Pyongyang's public image. The US Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), the Secret Service and cyber analysts have said North Korea orchestrated the hack, which has been described as the largest in history. This is the latest hack to be linked to North Korea, which has been accused of relying on cyber-crime to help finance its sanctioned economy. Blockchain analysts and the FBI have said the attack was led by state-backed hacking group TraderTraitor. The FBI has called on industry partners to help block transactions involving cryptocurrency accounts linked to the group. "The US has made a trite provocation of linking it with the Democratic People's Republic of Korea again," Kim Yo-jong, the director of North Korea's General Affairs Department, said in a statement. "It is a grave political provocation against the DPRK that the US misleads the international public opinion as if all the cyber crimes in different parts of the world are our deeds," she said. Why North Korea's 'elite' hackers are the prime suspect in major Binance hack Who could be behind the Binance hack and what we know so far But Pyongyang has been blamed for a number of major cyber attacks in recent years - accusations that it has denied. The TraderTraitor unit, which is also known as the Lazarus Group, was blamed for a then-record $1.5bn hack of crypto exchange Bybit in 2025. Pyongyang has systematically built its cyber operations, recruiting promising students from universities and sending them to hacker units overseen by North Korea's intelligence agency, research groups like the S Rajaratnam School of International Studies think tank have said. The country has consistently denied such claims. Kim Yo Jong said "it is the consistent policy stand of the DPRK government to resolutely oppose all sorts of malicious acts in cyberspace". Binance did not respond to the BBC's queries about North Korea's alleged involvement in the hack. Since the incident, the crypto giant has largely focused its public statements on the technical nature of the breach and its response to protect users. The company's spokesperson said that a net $4.72bn has been withdrawn from the exchange since transactions resumed on Sunday. The net outflow represents a "relatively limited portion" of Binance's total assets, which stand at approximately $157bn, the spokesperson told the BBC on Tuesday. That figure reflects the impact of the hack, subsequent withdrawals and market price changes. The company said last week that initial checks indicated that an engineer's laptop had been compromised, enabling an attacker to make unauthorised withdrawals. Trading in major cryptocurrencies on Binance has since resumed after the exchange worked with issuers to freeze assets impacted by the hack. The company has repeatedly said it would cover all of the losses linked to the attack and that it has so far covered around 95% of the assets stolen in the breach. Control of the Senate was still too close to call heading into the evening hours Tuesday. Trading in major cryptocurrencies on Binance has since resumed after the exchange worked with issuers to freeze assets impacted by the hack.
The TraderTraitor unit, which is also known as the Lazarus Group, was blamed for a then-record $1.5bn hack of crypto exchange Bybit in 2025.
An engineer was contacted through a legitimate job-hunting platform and invited to bogus job interviews with fake company representatives, Binance says.
If the accusations are true, the record-making heist shows how powerful suspected North Korean hackers have become.

sources.title: Google will let schools disable its AI tools, but not without sacrificing Search - TechCrunch
passages: Google announced on Tuesday that it plans to disable AI tools for K-12 students next year unless school administrators explicitly turn them on.
The tech giant says the change follows consultations with schools, teachers, leading researchers, and policymakers.
As a result, Google is revising its approach across Gemini, NotebookLM, Gemini in Classroom, and Google Search.

Chris Phillips, vice president for education at Google, told The New York Times that “Search and AI are deeply integrated,” which means that if a school chooses to restrict AI altogether, students “will not have access to search, and they’ll see a message from their school that indicates it’s not available.”
However, Google Search and its AI features are now inseparable.
Given the dominance of Google’s suite of apps in classrooms and the widespread use of Chromebooks, the decision underscores the company’s influence over the education sector.
Google announced the upcoming change alongside the launch of Guided Learning in schools.
The tool, which was unveiled earlier this year, sort of functions like an AI tutor, as it’s designed to help users build a deep understanding instead of just getting answers.
The launch comes amid concerns that AI chatbots undermine the learning process because they spit out direct answers.

Although teachers may not want students to use AI Overviews in Google Search to conduct research or complete assignments, they likely still want them to be able to have access to the search engine to find sources and other learning materials.

passages: The New York Times earlier reported that schools that turned off AI access entirely would not have access to Google search.

Amid outcry from educators about tech in classrooms, Google said Tuesday that artificial-intelligence tools, including the chatbot Gemini, will be disabled by default on K-12 student accounts, unless administrators choose to turn them on.

A Washington Post-Schar School poll of Kansas voters last week found registered Democrats were more than twice as likely as registered Republicans to complete the survey after answering an interviewer’s call — 32 percent versus 12 percent.
Google search typically includes an AI overview that, if expanded, has a chat window for further questions.
“Google is trying to use its monopoly power to force AI into our public schools,” New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani (D) said on X.
“No corporation should have the power to dictate how we teach our children.”
Google says the move responds to feedback from parents and teachers who say that AI products have been disastrous for the ability of children to learn and to think critically.
Google did not immediately return a request for comment.

sources.title: Google plans to shut off search access at schools that don’t allow AI tools - The Globe and Mail
passages: Students using Google software in the classroom will not be allowed to access the company’s search engine unless their school system also opts in to artificial intelligence tools, the tech giant said Tuesday.
On Tuesday, the company said that practice would no longer be the default option for school administrators.
Instead, K-12 schools will be able to individually turn each Google tool on or off – including Gemini, Gemini Notebook and search – with each being off by default until administrators turn it on.
But because search is integrated with AI, schools that opt out of AI altogether would also lose access to Google search.
“Because AI isn’t safe for kids and undermines education and critical thinking, schools should turn off Google’s AI tools the minute that option becomes available,” Golin said in a statement.
“Google is using its search monopoly to coerce schools into adopting AI.
This highlights the danger of allowing an unregulated monopolist to control an essential service,” wrote Lina Khan, former chair of the Federal Trade Commission, on social media.
“As the public increasingly pushes back against the use of AI in schools, Google is making clear it will punish those who don’t fall in line.”
\nThis is a space where subscribers can engage with each other and newsroom staff at The Globe and Mail.

Rather than fret about losing access to search, Golin urged schools to turn off not just AI but also Google, and “use this opportunity to help students find more privacy-protective alternatives for search, as well as ways to do more substantive research beyond search and click.”
All comments are subject to the Community Guidelines and are moderated. \n

The company also said it is updating its search tools to make them “better for learning,” including offering step-by-step guided learning through problems, so that students don’t get quick answers to school work.
Google is by far the dominant provider of education technology for U.S. schools.
Worldwide, the company says 150 million students and teachers use its Google Classroom platform, and many students use school-provided Chromebook computers.
But turning off AI altogether is not possible if schools want to use Google products.

New York City and Los Angeles, home to the nation’s biggest school districts, have issued temporary bans on generative AI tools in elementary and middle schools as they assess AI use and safety and develop policies on its use.
Google has not yet responded to messages seeking additional comments.

As a result, Google is revising its approach across Gemini, NotebookLM, Gemini in Classroom, and Google Search.

Chris Phillips, vice president for education at Google, told The New York Times that “Search and AI are deeply integrated,” which means that if a school chooses to restrict AI altogether, students “will not have access to search, and they’ll see a message from their school that indicates it’s not available.”
However, Google Search and its AI features are now inseparable.
Given the dominance of Google’s suite of apps in classrooms and the widespread use of Chromebooks, the decision underscores the company’s influence over the education sector.

Although teachers may not want students to use AI Overviews in Google Search to conduct research or complete assignments, they likely still want them to be able to have access to the search engine to find sources and other learning materials.

sources.title: Google will let schools skip AI tools, but they have to give up search, too
passages: Google is betting that schools won’t want to give up Google Search and will therefore accept AI tools.
This will expose students to AI early and often, possibly changing the way they interact with technology.
Schools that don’t like Google’s approach could switch to alternatives like DuckDuckGo, which lets you disable AI features.
But will Google’s new Guided Learning be enough to assuage their concerns?
Google will offer schools AI tools that purportedly don’t give away the answers.
While Google is trying to move beyond Chromebooks , the ubiquity of these devices has made the company’s education products huge in schools.
Now, Google says it will let educators choose whether to allow its AI tools in the classroom.
However, blocking AI tools also means giving up search, leaving schools with a difficult decision.
Google could make a version of search for schools that doesn’t have AI tools, but it’s not doing that.
Instead, it’s creating two different versions of AI in search.
The latter, available in Classroom as well as search, is supposed to provide one-on-one tutoring and assistance without giving away all the answers.
Google notes all of its generative AI products can make “mistakes,” though, so it may not be difficult to talk the chatbot into doing your homework.
In a statement to The New York Times , Google education VP Chris Phillips reiterated this approach to web search.
Google executives have said in no uncertain terms that Google Search is AI search .
Most searches now provide an AI Overview at the top, and the company is constantly coming up with new ways to nudge people toward the conversational AI Mode chatbot function.
When you look at what Google considers to be an AI tool, the nature of the Faustian bargain becomes clear.
The affected products are Gemini, Gemini Notebook, Gemini in Classroom, and Google Search .
There’s no picking and choosing—you either allow all the AI or none of it.

sources.title: Google plans to shut off search access at schools that don’t allow AI tools - The Globe and Mail
passages: Students using Google software in the classroom will not be allowed to access the company’s search engine unless their school system also opts in to artificial intelligence tools, the tech giant said Tuesday.
On Tuesday, the company said that practice would no longer be the default option for school administrators.
Instead, K-12 schools will be able to individually turn each Google tool on or off – including Gemini, Gemini Notebook and search – with each being off by default until administrators turn it on.
But because search is integrated with AI, schools that opt out of AI altogether would also lose access to Google search.
“Because AI isn’t safe for kids and undermines education and critical thinking, schools should turn off Google’s AI tools the minute that option becomes available,” Golin said in a statement.
“Google is using its search monopoly to coerce schools into adopting AI.
This highlights the danger of allowing an unregulated monopolist to control an essential service,” wrote Lina Khan, former chair of the Federal Trade Commission, on social media.
“As the public increasingly pushes back against the use of AI in schools, Google is making clear it will punish those who don’t fall in line.”
\nThis is a space where subscribers can engage with each other and newsroom staff at The Globe and Mail.

Rather than fret about losing access to search, Golin urged schools to turn off not just AI but also Google, and “use this opportunity to help students find more privacy-protective alternatives for search, as well as ways to do more substantive research beyond search and click.”
All comments are subject to the Community Guidelines and are moderated. \n

The company also said it is updating its search tools to make them “better for learning,” including offering step-by-step guided learning through problems, so that students don’t get quick answers to school work.
Google is by far the dominant provider of education technology for U.S. schools.
Worldwide, the company says 150 million students and teachers use its Google Classroom platform, and many students use school-provided Chromebook computers.
But turning off AI altogether is not possible if schools want to use Google products.

New York City and Los Angeles, home to the nation’s biggest school districts, have issued temporary bans on generative AI tools in elementary and middle schools as they assess AI use and safety and develop policies on its use.
Google has not yet responded to messages seeking additional comments.

passages: The tech giant announced on Tuesday that K-12 students won't have access to Google search if their school's AI functions are turned off. Jeff Chiu/The Associated Press

Students using Google software in the classroom will not be allowed to access the company’s search engine unless their school system also opts in to artificial intelligence tools, the tech giant said Tuesday.

The Mountain View, Calif., company has been facing pushback from educators, child development experts and parents over the use of its technology in schools, with the backlash heating up since it announced in August that it had turned on its Gemini chatbot for many K-12 students who use Google Classroom.

On Tuesday, the company said that practice would no longer be the default option for school administrators. Instead, K-12 schools will be able to individually turn each Google tool on or off – including Gemini, Gemini Notebook and search – with each being off by default until administrators turn it on. But because search is integrated with AI, schools that opt out of AI altogether would also lose access to Google search.
Canadian professors on how AI is changing education

“We believe schools should have control over AI in their classrooms and in providing administrators with controls to help them manage their approach,” Chris Phillips, Google’s vice president and general manager of education, said in a blog post.

The company also said it is updating its search tools to make them “better for learning,” including offering step-by-step guided learning through problems, so that students don’t get quick answers to school work.
But turning off AI altogether is not possible if schools want to use Google products.

Google is by far the dominant provider of education technology for U.S. schools. Worldwide, the company says 150 million students and teachers use its Google Classroom platform, and many students use school-provided Chromebook computers.
Tuesday’s announcement was met with swift criticism from educators and policy-makers.

“Google is using its search monopoly to coerce schools into adopting AI. This highlights the danger of allowing an unregulated monopolist to control an essential service,” wrote Lina Khan, former chair of the Federal Trade Commission, on social media. “As the public increasingly pushes back against the use of AI in schools, Google is making clear it will punish those who don’t fall in line.”
Lina Khan, former chair of the Federal Trade Commission, is among those criticizing Google's decision. POOL/Reuters
Google has not yet responded to messages seeking additional comments.

New York City and Los Angeles, home to the nation’s biggest school districts, have issued temporary bans on generative AI tools in elementary and middle schools as they assess AI use and safety and develop policies on its use.
Scientists push for creation of international body to regulate artificial intelligence

Many students already use AI to help with school and homework, but the technology has also made it easier to cheat and find quick, easy answers to questions instead of thinking critically. And experts have raised questions about how access to AI is affecting children’s brain development.

Josh Golin, executive director of children’s advocacy group Fairplay, said Google’s attempt to “strong-arm schools into using its AI products is likely to backfire.” He said Google’s technology in schools is not about learning but about “developing lifetime brand loyalty” for its products.
“Because AI isn’t safe for kids and undermines education and critical thinking, schools should turn off Google’s AI tools the minute that option becomes available,” Golin said in a statement.

Rather than fret about losing access to search, Golin urged schools to turn off not just AI but also Google, and “use this opportunity to help students find more privacy-protective alternatives for search, as well as ways to do more substantive research beyond search and click.”

sources.title: Data centers turn to commercial aircraft jet engines bolted onto trailers as AI power crunch bites — cast-off turbines generate up to 48 MW of electricity apiece - Tom's Hardware
passages: Faced with multi-year delays to secure grid power, US data center operators are deploying aeroderivative gas turbines — effectively retired commercial aircraft engines bolted into trailers — to keep AI infrastructure online.
According to IEEE Spectrum , facilities in Texas are already spinning up units based on General Electric’s CF6-80C2 and LM6000, the same turbine cores once found on 767s and Airbus A310s.

Vendors like ProEnergy and Mitsubishi Power have turned these into modular, fast-start generators capable of delivering 48 megawatts apiece, enough to support a large AI cluster while utility-scale infrastructure lags.
Tom's Hardware is part of Future US Inc, an international media group and leading digital publisher.

extraction.body: Stuck in years-long lines for grid connections and new turbines, some AI data centers are making their own electricity with converted jet engines, the New York Times reported Tuesday. The engines, pulled from retired aircraft and rebuilt to burn natural gas, aren’t anyone’s idea of a permanent power plant. But they’re another sign of how far power supply has fallen behind the AI buildout. For companies stuck in those lines, the main draw of converted jet engines is how quickly the engines can be up and running. “It’s all about getting power as fast as possible,” Rystad Energy analyst Audun Martinsen told the Times. With jet-powered units, “they can have a data center running in 24 months,” he said. Hooking up 100 megawatts to the grid in Northern Virginia, by comparison, takes about seven years , according to the International Energy Agency. Most power capacity is expected to come on by 2031, an executive at Mitsubishi Power, one of the world’s top makers of power generation equipment, told Bloomberg last week . In some cases, these delays are already costing some data center operators business. Last month, Microsoft pulled out as the anchor customer for Nscale’s data center in Loughton, England, after the local utility said it couldn’t deliver enough power until the early to mid-2030s. Elon Musk’s xAI is among the companies already using the engines, having installed eight converted jet-engine turbines in Mississippi to help power its Colossus 2 data center in Memphis, the Times reported, citing state permits and satellite imagery. The units come from ProEnergy, which rebuilds a GE engine commonly found on Boeing jets. In 2025, OpenAI followed Musk’s lead with gas turbines at its first Stargate site in Abilene, Texas. Crusoe, a Denver-based startup that builds AI data centers, is constructing that Abilene campus and ordered 13 of ProEnergy’s converted units in April. In September, Crusoe walked away from a $1.25 billion deal to buy 29 natural gas turbines from Boom Supersonic, a startup developing a supersonic passenger jet that has also begun selling a version of that jet’s engine as a power plant for data centers. A Crusoe spokesperson told TechCrunch at the time that the company still plans to use turbines. Currently the Trump administration is adding to the pressure by encouraging data centers to generate their own electricity. Converted jet engines come with trade-offs, though: They’re less efficient and pollute more than turbines designed for conventional gas plants, and it takes more of them to make the same amount of power, according to the Times. That may ultimately make converted jet engines a short-term play with some experts saying that efficiency and environmental concerns may grow in importance in a year or two. extraction.body: Artificial intelligence (AI) data centers are being built at an unprecedented pace. There are more than 12,000 active projects in the U.S. currently seeking grid interconnection representing 1,570 GW of generator capacity and 1,030 GW of energy storage. Analyst firm Omdia predicts that AI will drive more than 50% of installed power generation capacity over the next five years. A survey of energy industry stakeholders by Black & Veach found that lack of power was the biggest issue standing in the way of AI ambitions. 53% of utilities cited available power as the top obstacle to getting data centers online, with transmission (47%) and substation upgrades (46%) close behind. In response, data center developers have been gobbling up gas turbines. Some intend to power their own facilities while others are partnering with utilities to strengthen the ability of the grid in their areas to supply the energy needed for AI. Unfortunately, lead times on equipment are long and getting longer. “Orders for gas turbines today might not be delivered until 2032,” said Wes Cummins, chairman and CEO of Applied Digital, a data center developer and operator with multiple GW of data centers either operating, under construction, or in development. This includes two AI facilities operating in Ellendale and Harwood, North Dakota. He can’t afford to wait for gas turbines. His company has ordered 1.2 GW of steam turbines fed by gas-fired industrial boilers for another data center being built in North Dakota and two more are being finalized. Each will have this industrial boiler/steam turbine setup. The first one is scheduled to begin operation late in 2028. Applied Digital signed this $2.4 billion design/build agreement in conjunction with independent power producer Base Electron. extraction.body: As the world races to build the infrastructure behind artificial intelligence, data centers are hitting a critical energy roadblock. Across the U.S. and beyond, old airplane engines are being repurposed into power generators, keeping the AI boom from stalling.Data centers are expanding faster than utilities, with megawatt-hungry facilities waiting years to access grid power. Normally, developers would connect directly to the grid or build dedicated on-site power plants, but the surge in demand has exposed a deep supply shortage. Lead times for new gas turbines from manufacturers like GE, Vernova, and Siemens Energy now stretch from three to five years, sometimes even longer.“There just aren’t enough gas turbines to go around, and the problem is probably going to get worse,” says Paul Browning, CEO of Generative Power Solutions and former head of GE Power & Water and Mitsubishi Power, in an IEEE Spectrum report. Wood Mackenzie notes that lead times for new gas turbines are extending past 2029, while the Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis (IEEFA) reports backlogs of up to eight years for new plants in regions like Southeast Asia.This mismatch between demand and availability has created a new and flourishing market for refurbishing retired aircraft engines into fully functional power generators, known as aeroderivative gas turbines.A second life for jet enginesThough the demand is growing, the concept is not new. For decades, companies like GE Vernova and Siemens Energy have converted aviation engines for stationary power generation. These “aeroderivative” turbines are lighter, smaller, and easier to maintain than their heavy-frame industrial counterparts, making them ideal for temporary or mobile power setups.At the Data Center World Power show in San Antonio this October, Missouri-based energy firm ProEnergy showcased how it modernizes this approach. The company buys and overhauls used CF6-80C2 engine cores used in GE’s LM6000 and refits them into natural gas turbines branded as PE6000 units. Each refurbished unit can generate up to 48 megawatts (MW) of electricity, enough to power a small-to-medium data center or a town of 20,000 to 40,000 households.Landon Tessmer, Vice President of Commercial Operations at ProEnergy, told IEEE Spectrum that they have sold 21 gas turbines for two data-center projects, amounting to more than 1 gigawatt (GW). He adds, “Both projects are expected to provide bridging power for five to seven years, which is when they expect to have grid interconnection and no longer need permanent behind-the-meter generation.”Bridging power for the AI infra boomThese modified engines are an essential bridging technology. passages: As the world races to build the infrastructure behind artificial intelligence, data centers are hitting a critical energy roadblock.

Across the U.S. and beyond, old airplane engines are being repurposed into power generators, keeping the AI boom from stalling.Data centers are expanding faster than utilities, with megawatt-hungry facilities waiting years to access grid power.
Normally, developers would connect directly to the grid or build dedicated on-site power plants, but the surge in demand has exposed a deep supply shortage.

Lead times for new gas turbines from manufacturers like GE, Vernova, and Siemens Energy now stretch from three to five years, sometimes even longer.“There just aren’t enough gas turbines to go around, and the problem is probably going to get worse,” says Paul Browning, CEO of Generative Power Solutions and former head of GE Power & Water and Mitsubishi Power, in an IEEE Spectrum report.

Wood Mackenzie notes that lead times for new gas turbines are extending past 2029, while the Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis (IEEFA) reports backlogs of up to eight years for new plants in regions like Southeast Asia.This mismatch between demand and availability has created a new and flourishing market for refurbishing retired aircraft engines into fully functional power generators, known as aeroderivative gas turbines.A second life for jet enginesThough the demand is growing, the concept is not new.
For decades, companies like GE Vernova and Siemens Energy have converted aviation engines for stationary power generation.

These “aeroderivative” turbines are lighter, smaller, and easier to maintain than their heavy-frame industrial counterparts, making them ideal for temporary or mobile power setups.At the Data Center World Power show in San Antonio this October, Missouri-based energy firm ProEnergy showcased how it modernizes this approach.
The company buys and overhauls used CF6-80C2 engine cores used in GE’s LM6000 and refits them into natural gas turbines branded as PE6000 units.

Each refurbished unit can generate up to 48 megawatts (MW) of electricity, enough to power a small-to-medium data center or a town of 20,000 to 40,000 households.Landon Tessmer, Vice President of Commercial Operations at ProEnergy, told IEEE Spectrum that they have sold 21 gas turbines for two data-center projects, amounting to more than 1 gigawatt (GW).

With AI buildouts outpacing the grid, data centers are rolling in jet-powered turbines to keep their clusters online.
Meanwhile, Mitsubishi Power’s FT8 MOBILEPAC, which derives from Pratt & Whitney jet engines, delivers a similar output in a self-contained footprint designed for fast deployment.

For companies stuck in those lines, the main draw of converted jet engines is how quickly the engines can be up and running. “It’s all about getting power as fast as possible,” Rystad Energy analyst Audun Martinsen told the Times.
With jet-powered units, “they can have a data center running in 24 months,” he said.

In September, Crusoe walked away from a $1.25 billion deal to buy 29 natural gas turbines from Boom Supersonic, a startup developing a supersonic passenger jet that has also begun selling a version of that jet’s engine as a power plant for data centers.
Last month, Microsoft pulled out as the anchor customer for Nscale’s data center in Loughton, England, after the local utility said it couldn’t deliver enough power until the early to mid-2030s.

Each will have this industrial boiler/steam turbine setup.
Rentech has delivered more than 1,000 boilers and HRSGs across its 30-year history ranging from 20,000 to 650,000 pounds per hour of steam at pressures from 200 to 2,000 psi.
Lara said its models are best suited for steam turbines ranging from 10 MW to 20 MW, while modularized designs can accommodate turbines up to 50 MW, which are available from many different suppliers.
Similarly, a broad range of steam turbine manufacturers exists.
That year, close to 140 GW of steam turbines of at least 5 MW were manufactured.
That is already beginning to be the case for the very large steam turbines.
A record build-out of combined cycle power plants, too, means steam turbines larger than 300 MW are in demand.
However, there remains plenty of spare supply chain capacity among the mid-sized and smaller steam turbine sectors.
Global Market Insights predicts that the steam turbine market will grow by almost three times between 2025 and 2034.
The industrial boiler market is expected to see a similar growth trajectory.
53% of utilities cited available power as the top obstacle to getting data centers online, with transmission (47%) and substation upgrades (46%) close behind.

“Orders for gas turbines today might not be delivered until 2032,” said Wes Cummins, chairman and CEO of Applied Digital, a data center developer and operator with multiple GW of data centers either operating, under construction, or in development.
Water inside the boiler tubes is turned into steam.
Steam turbines and package boilers offer immediate advantages.
Industrial boilers have been around for so long that the supply chain and manufacturing capacity is extensive.
Expect to see boiler manufacturers stepping up output rapidly to capitalize on the lack of power availability from many other sectors.
Boiler steam will supplement the steam produced using exhaust heat from the gas turbine in a heat recovery steam generator (HRSG).
Other suppliers such as Siemens Energy, Solar Turbines, and Mitsubishi Power report similar supply delays.

Wood Mackenzie notes that lead times for new gas turbines are extending past 2029, while the Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis (IEEFA) reports backlogs of up to eight years for new plants in regions like Southeast Asia.This mismatch between demand and availability has created a new and flourishing market for refurbishing retired aircraft engines into fully functional power generators, known as aeroderivative gas turbines.A second life for jet enginesThough the demand is growing, the concept is not new.

Across the U.S. and beyond, old airplane engines are being repurposed into power generators, keeping the AI boom from stalling.Data centers are expanding faster than utilities, with megawatt-hungry facilities waiting years to access grid power.
For decades, companies like GE Vernova and Siemens Energy have converted aviation engines for stationary power generation.

These “aeroderivative” turbines are lighter, smaller, and easier to maintain than their heavy-frame industrial counterparts, making them ideal for temporary or mobile power setups.At the Data Center World Power show in San Antonio this October, Missouri-based energy firm ProEnergy showcased how it modernizes this approach.
Normally, developers would connect directly to the grid or build dedicated on-site power plants, but the surge in demand has exposed a deep supply shortage.

According to IEEE Spectrum , facilities in Texas are already spinning up units based on General Electric’s CF6-80C2 and LM6000, the same turbine cores once found on 767s and Airbus A310s.

Vendors like ProEnergy and Mitsubishi Power have turned these into modular, fast-start generators capable of delivering 48 megawatts apiece, enough to support a large AI cluster while utility-scale infrastructure lags.

extraction.body: Stuck in years-long lines for grid connections and new turbines, some AI data centers are making their own electricity with converted jet engines, the New York Times reported Tuesday. The engines, pulled from retired aircraft and rebuilt to burn natural gas, aren’t anyone’s idea of a permanent power plant. But they’re another sign of how far power supply has fallen behind the AI buildout. For companies stuck in those lines, the main draw of converted jet engines is how quickly the engines can be up and running. “It’s all about getting power as fast as possible,” Rystad Energy analyst Audun Martinsen told the Times. With jet-powered units, “they can have a data center running in 24 months,” he said. Hooking up 100 megawatts to the grid in Northern Virginia, by comparison, takes about seven years , according to the International Energy Agency. Most power capacity is expected to come on by 2031, an executive at Mitsubishi Power, one of the world’s top makers of power generation equipment, told Bloomberg last week . In some cases, these delays are already costing some data center operators business. Last month, Microsoft pulled out as the anchor customer for Nscale’s data center in Loughton, England, after the local utility said it couldn’t deliver enough power until the early to mid-2030s. Elon Musk’s xAI is among the companies already using the engines, having installed eight converted jet-engine turbines in Mississippi to help power its Colossus 2 data center in Memphis, the Times reported, citing state permits and satellite imagery. The units come from ProEnergy, which rebuilds a GE engine commonly found on Boeing jets. In 2025, OpenAI followed Musk’s lead with gas turbines at its first Stargate site in Abilene, Texas. Crusoe, a Denver-based startup that builds AI data centers, is constructing that Abilene campus and ordered 13 of ProEnergy’s converted units in April. In September, Crusoe walked away from a $1.25 billion deal to buy 29 natural gas turbines from Boom Supersonic, a startup developing a supersonic passenger jet that has also begun selling a version of that jet’s engine as a power plant for data centers. A Crusoe spokesperson told TechCrunch at the time that the company still plans to use turbines. Currently the Trump administration is adding to the pressure by encouraging data centers to generate their own electricity. Converted jet engines come with trade-offs, though: They’re less efficient and pollute more than turbines designed for conventional gas plants, and it takes more of them to make the same amount of power, according to the Times. That may ultimately make converted jet engines a short-term play with some experts saying that efficiency and environmental concerns may grow in importance in a year or two. extraction.body: Artificial intelligence (AI) data centers are being built at an unprecedented pace. There are more than 12,000 active projects in the U.S. currently seeking grid interconnection representing 1,570 GW of generator capacity and 1,030 GW of energy storage. Analyst firm Omdia predicts that AI will drive more than 50% of installed power generation capacity over the next five years. A survey of energy industry stakeholders by Black & Veach found that lack of power was the biggest issue standing in the way of AI ambitions. 53% of utilities cited available power as the top obstacle to getting data centers online, with transmission (47%) and substation upgrades (46%) close behind. In response, data center developers have been gobbling up gas turbines. Some intend to power their own facilities while others are partnering with utilities to strengthen the ability of the grid in their areas to supply the energy needed for AI. Unfortunately, lead times on equipment are long and getting longer. “Orders for gas turbines today might not be delivered until 2032,” said Wes Cummins, chairman and CEO of Applied Digital, a data center developer and operator with multiple GW of data centers either operating, under construction, or in development. This includes two AI facilities operating in Ellendale and Harwood, North Dakota. He can’t afford to wait for gas turbines. His company has ordered 1.2 GW of steam turbines fed by gas-fired industrial boilers for another data center being built in North Dakota and two more are being finalized. Each will have this industrial boiler/steam turbine setup. The first one is scheduled to begin operation late in 2028. Applied Digital signed this $2.4 billion design/build agreement in conjunction with independent power producer Base Electron. extraction.body: As the world races to build the infrastructure behind artificial intelligence, data centers are hitting a critical energy roadblock. Across the U.S. and beyond, old airplane engines are being repurposed into power generators, keeping the AI boom from stalling.Data centers are expanding faster than utilities, with megawatt-hungry facilities waiting years to access grid power. Normally, developers would connect directly to the grid or build dedicated on-site power plants, but the surge in demand has exposed a deep supply shortage. Lead times for new gas turbines from manufacturers like GE, Vernova, and Siemens Energy now stretch from three to five years, sometimes even longer.“There just aren’t enough gas turbines to go around, and the problem is probably going to get worse,” says Paul Browning, CEO of Generative Power Solutions and former head of GE Power & Water and Mitsubishi Power, in an IEEE Spectrum report. Wood Mackenzie notes that lead times for new gas turbines are extending past 2029, while the Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis (IEEFA) reports backlogs of up to eight years for new plants in regions like Southeast Asia.This mismatch between demand and availability has created a new and flourishing market for refurbishing retired aircraft engines into fully functional power generators, known as aeroderivative gas turbines.A second life for jet enginesThough the demand is growing, the concept is not new. For decades, companies like GE Vernova and Siemens Energy have converted aviation engines for stationary power generation. These “aeroderivative” turbines are lighter, smaller, and easier to maintain than their heavy-frame industrial counterparts, making them ideal for temporary or mobile power setups.At the Data Center World Power show in San Antonio this October, Missouri-based energy firm ProEnergy showcased how it modernizes this approach. The company buys and overhauls used CF6-80C2 engine cores used in GE’s LM6000 and refits them into natural gas turbines branded as PE6000 units. Each refurbished unit can generate up to 48 megawatts (MW) of electricity, enough to power a small-to-medium data center or a town of 20,000 to 40,000 households.Landon Tessmer, Vice President of Commercial Operations at ProEnergy, told IEEE Spectrum that they have sold 21 gas turbines for two data-center projects, amounting to more than 1 gigawatt (GW). He adds, “Both projects are expected to provide bridging power for five to seven years, which is when they expect to have grid interconnection and no longer need permanent behind-the-meter generation.”Bridging power for the AI infra boomThese modified engines are an essential bridging technology. Across the U.S. and beyond, old airplane engines are being repurposed into power generators, keeping the AI boom from stalling.Data centers are expanding faster than utilities, with megawatt-hungry facilities waiting years to access grid power.
Normally, developers would connect directly to the grid or build dedicated on-site power plants, but the surge in demand has exposed a deep supply shortage.

Lead times for new gas turbines from manufacturers like GE, Vernova, and Siemens Energy now stretch from three to five years, sometimes even longer.“There just aren’t enough gas turbines to go around, and the problem is probably going to get worse,” says Paul Browning, CEO of Generative Power Solutions and former head of GE Power & Water and Mitsubishi Power, in an IEEE Spectrum report.

passages: Chris Phillips, Google's vice president and general manager of education, said in a blog post that Search, along with Google's Gemini chatbot, Gemini Notebook and Gemini in Google Classroom, will be set off by default for K-12 student accounts until school administrators turn them on.

The company said it would share more specifics with schools "in the coming months" ahead of the rollout and that the decision followed conversations with schools, teachers, researchers and policymakers.

(Bloomberg) -- Schools that want their K-12 students to have access to Google Search will soon have to turn it on themselves, and the AI features built into Search will come with it, under changes the Alphabet Inc. company announced Tuesday.
The company also said Guided Learning, a study mode Google first released in its Gemini app, would be extended into Search.
When Google's systems detect a student is looking for certain types of homework help, Search will walk them through a problem one step at a time.
A student who pastes in a physics problem or asks for help with a book report, for example, will get prompts meant to make them work through the concepts instead of skipping to the answer.
The change comes as Google, whose Chromebooks are the most widely used laptops in American classrooms, faces growing resistance to AI from parents and school districts.
Google will pilot Guided Learning within Google Search in select US schools later this month and plans to expand it to other districts after collecting feedback from teachers.

sources.title: Google will let schools disable its AI tools, but not without sacrificing Search
passages: Google announced on Tuesday that it plans to disable AI tools for K-12 students next year unless school administrators explicitly turn them on.
The tech giant says the change follows consultations with schools, teachers, leading researchers, and policymakers.
As a result, Google is revising its approach across Gemini, NotebookLM, Gemini in Classroom, and Google Search.

Chris Phillips, vice president for education at Google, told The New York Times that “Search and AI are deeply integrated,” which means that if a school chooses to restrict AI altogether, students “will not have access to search, and they’ll see a message from their school that indicates it’s not available.”
However, Google Search and its AI features are now inseparable.
Given the dominance of Google’s suite of apps in classrooms and the widespread use of Chromebooks, the decision underscores the company’s influence over the education sector.
Google announced the upcoming change alongside the launch of Guided Learning in schools.
The tool, which was unveiled earlier this year, sort of functions like an AI tutor, as it’s designed to help users build a deep understanding instead of just getting answers.
The launch comes amid concerns that AI chatbots undermine the learning process because they spit out direct answers.

Although teachers may not want students to use AI Overviews in Google Search to conduct research or complete assignments, they likely still want them to be able to have access to the search engine to find sources and other learning materials.

extraction.body: Starting early 2027, Gemini and Google Search become opt-in for student accounts, and schools can't keep one without the other Tue 3 Nov 2026 · 11:32 EST · 4 min read Google is about to give school administrators a choice that isn’t really much of a choice. Starting early next year, its AI tools will be turned off by default for K-12 student accounts, and schools that keep AI disabled will lose Google Search along with it. That means a district that wants to keep chatbots out of the classroom may also have to keep the world’s most popular search engine out. Google announced the policy on Tuesday, November 3, 2026. The changes apply to student accounts within Google Workspace for Education, the software suite many US schools rely on for email, documents and classwork. Beginning in early 2027, access to Gemini, Gemini Notebook and Google Search will be opt-in. The default setting will be disabled. School administrators will need to actively turn these tools on if they want students to use them. Doing nothing means students get nothing. The catch is how tightly Google has woven AI into search itself. Features like AI Overviews and AI Mode now sit inside the core search experience, so Google says it can’t cleanly separate the two. Google VP Chris Phillips emphasized that integration when explaining the decision. According to the research findings, Phillips indicated there will be no granular controls that let schools switch off AI Overviews alone while keeping standard search running. Google says it plans to share more detailed implementation information in the coming months. The move lands in the middle of a broader backlash against generative AI in classrooms. Educators and policymakers have raised concerns about cheating and student privacy as AI tools spread through schools faster than rules could keep up. Daily. Free. Join 34,000+ readers across crypto, finance, and policy. We respect your privacy. Unsubscribe anytime. Several major US districts have already drawn hard lines. Los Angeles Unified announced a moratorium on generative AI across all grades in early September 2026. New York City has placed limits on AI usage in schools through 8th grade. That covers the country’s largest school system for most of its younger students. Frederick County’s school district went further on October 7, 2026, voting to ban generative AI from pre-K through 12th grade. Those decisions were made before Google’s announcement. Now each of those districts faces a new question: does a ban on generative AI also mean a ban on Google Search? Google isn’t only flipping switches. The company plans to pilot a feature called Guided Learning, designed to encourage students to work through problems rather than receive instant answers. The idea is to make AI behave more like a tutor than an answer key. Instead of spitting out the solution to a math problem, the tool would nudge students toward reasoning it out themselves. The most immediate impact falls on school administrators, who now carry the decision explicitly. Under the new default, inaction disables AI and search, so districts can’t simply let the status quo ride. That shifts accountability in a notable way. If AI shows up in a classroom, it’s because a school chose it, not because Google pushed it there by default. For districts with existing bans, the tradeoff is steeper. Los Angeles Unified, New York City and Frederick County will each need to decide whether their AI restrictions are worth losing Google Search for students, or whether to revisit the scope of those policies. The no-granular-controls position is likely to be the most debated part of the plan. Schools that are comfortable with traditional search but wary of AI summaries have no middle option under the approach Phillips described. The broader signal is about how far AI has spread into everyday software. Google’s position is that AI and search are now effectively the same product. The catch is how tightly Google has woven AI into search itself. Features like AI Overviews and AI Mode now sit inside the core search experience, so Google says it can’t cleanly separate the two.

Google VP Chris Phillips emphasized that integration when explaining the decision. According to the research findings, Phillips indicated there will be no granular controls that let schools switch off AI Overviews alone while keeping standard search running.
Google says it plans to share more detailed implementation information in the coming months.

The move lands in the middle of a broader backlash against generative AI in classrooms. Educators and policymakers have raised concerns about cheating and student privacy as AI tools spread through schools faster than rules could keep up.
