extraction.body: COPENHAGEN, Nov 3 (Reuters) – Greenland’s parliament on Tuesday ratified the Arctic island’s security agreement struck earlier this year with US President Donald Trump, although some opposition party members questioned the deal’s economic value. The United States, Denmark and Greenland in September signed the agreement, aimed at ending tensions after Trump’s repeated threats to take control of the strategically located and mineral-rich island, a self-governing Danish territory. The deal expands the US military’s role in Greenland, paving the way for two new military bases and Trump’s “Golden Dome” missile defence system, while reaffirming Danish sovereignty and Greenlanders’ right to self-determination. A majority of lawmakers had already signalled support for the deal in a first debate last month. Tuesday’s vote was 16 in favour and none against, with 7 abstentions. The White House in January said Trump was discussing options for acquiring Greenland, including potential use of the US military, alarming governments in Europe and triggering intense diplomatic efforts to calm the situation. Greenlandic Foreign Minister Mute Egede said on Tuesday that ratification of the deal was an important step for the island. “We must accept that peace and stability are no longer something we can take for granted,” Egede told lawmakers in Nuuk shortly before the vote. Opposition party Naleraq, the most prominent political voice for Greenland’s independence, questioned the deal’s economic value during the debate. “We are looking for a better agreement that we can benefit from when we become an independent state. But no economic benefit has been gained from the agreement,” Naleraq chair Pele Broberg said. The Danish parliament is due to give the bill a first reading on November 11, followed by a second reading and a vote on November 19. The executive agreement will enter into force once Denmark and Greenland have ratified it, and does not require approval from the US Senate. (Reporting by Louise Rasmussen and Stine Jacobsen, editing by Terje Solsvik and Gareth Jones) Disclaimer: This report is auto generated from the Reuters news service. sources.title: Greenland's parliament ratifies Trump's trilateral security agreement, expanding US military presence - DW.com
passages: Greenland's parliament on Tuesday signed off on a trilateral security and military-access agreement with the United States and Denmark that paves the way for an expanded US' military presence on the strategically located and mineral-rich island.
The agreement allows for two new US military bases and Trump's "Golden Dome" missile defence system.
It also keeps Greenland under Danish control, while reaffirming Greenlanders' right to self determination.
In January 2026, Trump began calling for the US to control Greenland, and threatened the use of military force and tariffs against US European allies if he did not get his way.
Under a 1951 agreement, the US already has considerable military freedom of action in Greenland.
After years of voluntarily drawing down its military presence, the US only maintains the Pituffik Space Base in northwestern Greenland, which is used for missile defense and radar surveillance.

After months of negotiation the agreement was signed in September by Trump, Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen and Greenlandic Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York.
Critics have pointed out the same deal could have been made without the extreme disruption caused by Trump's territorial and tariff threats.
Pele Broberg, chair of the pro-independence Naleraq party, questioned the deal's value for Greenland.
The agreement will come into effect after ratification by the Danish parliament, which is due to read the bill over two sessions in November.
Trump had claimed that Denmark was not doing enough to defend its autonomous arctic territory from unspecified threats from China and Russia.

sources.title: Ford Privacy Promise Gives Owners Control Over Connected Car Data
passages: Ford has introduced a new Privacy Promise, publicly committing to protect customer vehicle data and give owners greater control over the information they share.

Jones reiterated that Ford's objective is to offer products and services that provide value to customers, not to monetize their personal information..Privacy Resources to Expand Beyond US.Ford said the Privacy Promise website will provide information about its privacy practices and available controls.

Customers can learn what information Ford collects, how it is used, and how they can opt in or out of data sharing.Kristin Jones, Ford's Chief Privacy Officer, said the company wants to communicate its data practices more clearly and help customers understand their privacy choices.The announcement comes as automakers introduce increasingly connected vehicles with features such as remote start, navigation, and driver-assistance technology.

She also noted that automakers were viewed as more trusted custodians of privacy than several other large organizations handling personal information..Turning Off Data Sharing Could Affect Connected Features.Ford said customers can manage their data-sharing preferences through their vehicle's center display.

sources.title: Ford Introduces the Ford Privacy Promise to Protect Customer Data - DBusiness Magazine
passages: Ford Motor Co. in Dearborn is launching the Ford Privacy Promise to make an “explicit commitment to customers that their vehicle data is safe” and they’re in control of what they share.
As Ford created the Privacy Promise, it surveyed more than 1,000 U.S. consumers — both Ford and non-Ford owners.
It learned that while privacy is important to them, customers understand the value of data sharing.

“Even for a tech-savvy consumer, it can be hard to understand the relationship between your vehicle, the data it generates, and your privacy and rights,” says Kristin Jones, chief privacy officer and deputy general counsel for data and privacy at Ford.
“With our connected vehicle and app user communities growing every day, Ford takes its responsibility in safeguarding customer data seriously.”
Ford says it designs and builds its products with privacy in mind — from collection of data to its use, storage, and disposal.
This can include privacy-enhancing technologies like anonymizing or aggregating data to further protect a customer’s privacy.
As a result, Ford offers vehicle privacy settings that allow customers to control what data they want to share, subject to the features and services they wish to enjoy.
Ford stresses that it never sells data about how customers drive their vehicle to data brokers.

sources.title: Ford Makes a Privacy Promise as GM Pays $220 Million Over Driver Data - MotorBiscuit
passages: Data privacy has become an uncomfortable subject for America’s automakers.
Within days of General Motors agreeing to a $220 million settlement over how it handled driver information, Ford announced a new customer-facing commitment on the same issue.
GM must now restrict the driving data it collects and obtain a driver’s explicit consent before gathering or sharing it.
According to a report by MotorBiscuit , an outside party will also audit its privacy programs.
Earlier, in January 2025, it agreed with the Federal Trade Commission to stop sharing geolocation and driving-behavior data with consumer reporting agencies for five years.
It is not yet clear whether affected owners will receive any of the $220 million.
Against that backdrop, Ford has introduced the Ford Privacy Promise, which is meant to assure owners that their information is protected and that they decide what to share.
The data came from Smart Driver, a program that enrolled millions of motorists from 2016 until GM discontinued it in 2024.
To support the effort, Ford surveyed more than 1,000 U.S. customers about their understanding of data privacy.
Respondents overwhelmingly said they want the ability to control and adjust their privacy settings whenever they choose.
Ford says it develops its products with privacy in mind and tries to make clear how personal details are used.

Within days of General Motors agreeing to a $220 million settlement over how it handled driver information, Ford announced a new customer-facing commitment on the same issue. The contrast is hard to miss. GM stood accused of letting driving data reach insurance companies, while Ford is now telling owners that they decide what their vehicles share. Here is what led to the settlement, and what Ford is promising in response. The data came from Smart Driver, a program that enrolled millions of motorists from 2016 until GM discontinued it in 2024. Many participants also subscribed to OnStar. GM must now restrict the driving data it collects and obtain a driver’s explicit consent before gathering or sharing it. According to a report by MotorBiscuit , an outside party will also audit its privacy programs. GM said the agreement reinforces steps it has already taken. This is not the company’s first penalty on the subject. It paid $12.75 million to settle a California investigation in May. Earlier, in January 2025, it agreed with the Federal Trade Commission to stop sharing geolocation and driving-behavior data with consumer reporting agencies for five years. It is not yet clear whether affected owners will receive any of the $220 million. According to Ford Authority , Ford maintains that it does not sell driving data to third parties, although a recent study found that it shares some personal vehicle data with outside companies. Against that backdrop, Ford has introduced the Ford Privacy Promise, which is meant to assure owners that their information is protected and that they decide what to share. The company has built a dedicated website explaining how to change data settings, either inside the vehicle or through the Ford App. Ford says it develops its products with privacy in mind and tries to make clear how personal details are used. The pledge also states that Ford never sells data on how customers drive to data brokers. That is the practice at the center of GM’s legal trouble. extraction.body: Modern vehicles can record far more than mileage and fuel consumption. From acceleration and braking habits to location history, connected cars generate information that could reveal how, when, and where their owners drive. Sure, that technology can make vehicles safer and more convenient, but it also raises uncomfortable questions about who actually controls the information. Drivers may not always understand what they're sharing or how it could eventually be used. Automotive privacy has been under scrutiny lately, particularly where insurance companies are concerned, following a major settlement involving General Motors and the sale of customer driving data . Now, Ford is making its own position explicit through a new initiative called the Privacy Promise , which explains how customers can manage connected-vehicle information and what Ford says it will never sell. On October 29, GM agreed to pay $220 million to resolve allegations brought by a coalition of 36 state attorneys general. Investigators found that its Smart Driver program collected driving and location information that was sold to data brokers and subsequently made available to insurers. The information included speeding, hard braking, acceleration, and individual trip records, potentially influencing insurance premiums. The settlement also requires GM to obtain express consent before collecting or disclosing certain driving and location data. Ford's new policy explicitly states that it does not sell information about customers' driving behavior to data brokers. The company also says it designs its connected services around privacy protections, including anonymizing or aggregating information where appropriate. Connected vehicles routinely collect diagnostic information, driving characteristics, and location data. Ford says it uses this information for navigation, roadside assistance, vehicle troubleshooting, product development, and personalized services. Ford says owners can review and change their privacy preferences through their vehicle's touchscreen or the Ford App. Drivers can also opt out of connected-vehicle data sharing entirely, although doing so disables certain functions. Those trade-offs include losing access to features such as BlueCruise, internet connectivity, and vehicle-location information in the app. Ford recommends that owners of vehicles built from 2018 onward check their settings. Ford surveyed just over 1,000 American consumers while developing the initiative and found that customers valued control over their information. The automaker plans to expand its privacy resources to Lincoln owners and additional markets. Ford's promise should offer some reassurance to owners concerned about how their driving data is being used. Still, it's worth checking the privacy settings in your vehicle to see exactly what information you're sharing and which features depend on it. As a result, Ford offers vehicle privacy settings that allow customers to control what data they want to share, subject to the features and services they wish to enjoy.
Ford stresses that it never sells data about how customers drive their vehicle to data brokers.

passages: On October 29, GM agreed to pay $220 million to resolve allegations brought by a coalition of 36 state attorneys general.

Ford's promise should offer some reassurance to owners concerned about how their driving data is being used.

extraction.body: Modern vehicles can record far more than mileage and fuel consumption. From acceleration and braking habits to location history, connected cars generate information that could reveal how, when, and where their owners drive. Sure, that technology can make vehicles safer and more convenient, but it also raises uncomfortable questions about who actually controls the information. Drivers may not always understand what they're sharing or how it could eventually be used. Automotive privacy has been under scrutiny lately, particularly where insurance companies are concerned, following a major settlement involving General Motors and the sale of customer driving data . Now, Ford is making its own position explicit through a new initiative called the Privacy Promise , which explains how customers can manage connected-vehicle information and what Ford says it will never sell. On October 29, GM agreed to pay $220 million to resolve allegations brought by a coalition of 36 state attorneys general. Investigators found that its Smart Driver program collected driving and location information that was sold to data brokers and subsequently made available to insurers. The information included speeding, hard braking, acceleration, and individual trip records, potentially influencing insurance premiums. The settlement also requires GM to obtain express consent before collecting or disclosing certain driving and location data. Ford's new policy explicitly states that it does not sell information about customers' driving behavior to data brokers. The company also says it designs its connected services around privacy protections, including anonymizing or aggregating information where appropriate. Connected vehicles routinely collect diagnostic information, driving characteristics, and location data. Ford says it uses this information for navigation, roadside assistance, vehicle troubleshooting, product development, and personalized services. Ford says owners can review and change their privacy preferences through their vehicle's touchscreen or the Ford App. Drivers can also opt out of connected-vehicle data sharing entirely, although doing so disables certain functions. Those trade-offs include losing access to features such as BlueCruise, internet connectivity, and vehicle-location information in the app. Ford recommends that owners of vehicles built from 2018 onward check their settings. Ford surveyed just over 1,000 American consumers while developing the initiative and found that customers valued control over their information. The automaker plans to expand its privacy resources to Lincoln owners and additional markets. Ford's promise should offer some reassurance to owners concerned about how their driving data is being used. Still, it's worth checking the privacy settings in your vehicle to see exactly what information you're sharing and which features depend on it. The PGA Tour remains in Mexico for the second straight week, shifting from Nuevo Vallarta, going northwest across the Gulf of California to Cabo San Lucas. It is the fourth edition of the World Wide Technology Championship to be held at the El Cardonal Course at the Diamante Resort, a Tiger Woods design, and it is the sixth of eight FedEx Cup Fall events in 2026. This is the first of the remaining three fall series tournaments for players to earn a spot in the top 100 of the FedExCup Standings and secure themselves a spot on Tour for the 2027 season. The RSM Classic at Sea Island in St. Simons Island, Georgia, is the final stop of the fall series, teeing off on Thursday, November 19. Here are those players currently ranked from 95-110 in the FedExCup Standings. (*denotes players who are exempt for 2027) 95. John Parry 96. Max Greyserman 97. Billy Horschel 98. Kevin Yu 99. Chandler Phillips 100. Jason Day 101. Mackenzie Hughes 102. Taylor Pendrith 103. Brandt Snedeker* 104. A.J. Ewart 105. Lee Hodges 106. Rasmus Neergaard-Petersen 107. Chandler Blanchet 108. Brooks Koepka* 109. Tony Finau* 110. Chris Kirk This golf course has proven to be one of the easier tracks on the Tour calendar. The average winning score over the first three times we have seen this course is nearly 27-under par. Ben Griffin is your defending champion, winning last fall with a score of 29-under. As at Vidanta Vallarta, El Cardonal’s main defense is the wind, given its location between the Gulf of California and the Pacific Ocean. However, the forecast looks tame, with high temperatures in the low 80s and light winds of 5-15 MPH. Also, like last week, the golf course is wall-to-wall Paspalum Grass with especially wide fairways and massive greens. For resort courses in windy locations, this design is not uncommon. It would be next to impossible for a typical resort guest to play a course in heavy winds without oversized fairways and greens. In addition, there is really no rough to speak of off the fairways at El Cardonal. Like these two Tour stops in Mexico, we see similar designs in potentially windy, resort locations like Kapalua, Southern Utah at the Black Desert Resort and the Dominican Republic at Corales Puntacana. The golf course is a Par 72 that measures close to 7,500 yards. I leaned heavily on Strokes Gained: Approach this week, along with Scrambling and Hole Proximity from 175 to 200+ yards. We got it done with Andrew Novak using a very similar formula last week, and I believe the puzzle is not all that different here. I also looked at Par 5 Scoring, Birdie or Better Percentage, 3-Putt Avoidance and Strokes Gained: Putting (Paspalum). I already made reference to a few of the courses that I believe provide correlation: The Plantation Course at Kapalua, the former home of the Sentry Tournament of Champions, Corales, Vidanta Vallarta and Black Desert. I also believe there are connections with TPC Summerlin, the former home of the Shriners Children’s Open in Las Vegas, Sea Island (RSM Classic) and the Grand Reserve Golf Club, where they play the Puerto Rico Open. I landed on Novak two weeks in a row and it worked, so let’s try again with the 19-year-old who was third earlier this season in Puerto Rico, 11th at Corales Puntacana and finished top-20 last week at Vidanta Vallarta – where off the tee he was brilliant, ranking eighth in Driving Distance and No. 1 in Driving Accuracy. Over the last 20 rounds, Brown ranks fifth in this field for SG: Approach and is 22nd in Scrambling. Fisk is another player who can putt, is very good with the long irons and is both long and straight off the tee. He closed with a 63 last week at Vidanta to finish runner-up to Novak. A month ago, he finished seventh at Black Desert. This is only Fisk’s second full season on Tour, and he already has two wins. Last season he finished fourth in Puerto Rico. Over the last 20 rounds, he ranks third in this field for Hole Proximity from 175-200 yards. It has been a minute since I have backed my fellow Las Vegas resident, but he seems to flourish in resort, coastal locations, with his last Tour victory coming at Port Royal Golf Club in Bermuda in 2022, where he just lost in a playoff two weeks ago. Power was 11th earlier this year at Corales Puntacana and has three top-10 finishes at Sea Island. Over the last 20 rounds, he ranks fifth in this field for Birdie or Better Percentage and is eighth in Scrambling. Here’s a guy who has won at both Sea Island and Kapalua. Kirk has two top-10 finishes in his last three starts, and as noted earlier, he currently sits at 110th in the FedEx Cup standings. With the way he is playing, he looks on track to crack the top 100 very soon. Over the last 20 rounds, Kirk is No. 1 in this field for SG: Approach, No. 2 on the Par 5s, 11th in Scrambling and ninth in 3-Putt Avoidance. Like Blades Brown, I’m going to give Clanton another go for the second week in a row. He is currently 123rd in the FedEx Cup Fall standings and has finished seventh, 11th and 29th in his last three starts. Clanton also finished fifth earlier this year in Puerto Rico and was runner-up at the 2024 RSM Classic. Over the last 20 rounds, he ranks sixth in this field for SG: Approach and is 17th for both Hole Proximity from 175-200 yards and in Scrambling. Clanton ranks 10th for SG: Par 5s and third for 3-Putt Avoidance. McGreevy sits in a similar spot in the standings to Clanton and has also been playing well lately, with two top-30 finishes in two recent starts. He was 26th at Black Desert a month ago, where he ranked eighth in that field for SG: Off the Tee. He was 29th last week at Vidanta, where he ranked fourth in that field for SG: Approach. Over the last 20 rounds, McGreevy ranks fifth in this field for Hole Proximity from 175-200 yards and is 21st in Scrambling. McGreevy was 11th earlier this season in Puerto Rico. He finished runner-up at Corales Puntacana in 2022 and was runner-up last year at the RSM Classic. He finished 11th at Black Desert in both 2024 and in 2025. Here are those players currently ranked from 95-110 in the FedExCup Standings. (*denotes players who are exempt for 2027)

95. John Parry 96. Max Greyserman 97. Billy Horschel 98. Kevin Yu 99. Chandler Phillips 100. Jason Day 101. Mackenzie Hughes 102. Taylor Pendrith 103. Brandt Snedeker* 104. A.J. Ewart 105. Lee Hodges 106. Rasmus Neergaard-Petersen 107. Chandler Blanchet 108. Brooks Koepka* 109. Tony Finau* 110. Chris Kirk

This golf course has proven to be one of the easier tracks on the Tour calendar. The average winning score over the first three times we have seen this course is nearly 27-under par. Ben Griffin is your defending champion, winning last fall with a score of 29-under. As at Vidanta Vallarta, El Cardonal’s main defense is the wind, given its location between the Gulf of California and the Pacific Ocean. However, the forecast looks tame, with high temperatures in the low 80s and light winds of 5-15 MPH.

Also, like last week, the golf course is wall-to-wall Paspalum Grass with especially wide fairways and massive greens. For resort courses in windy locations, this design is not uncommon. It would be next to impossible for a typical resort guest to play a course in heavy winds without oversized fairways and greens. In addition, there is really no rough to speak of off the fairways at El Cardonal. Like these two Tour stops in Mexico, we see similar designs in potentially windy, resort locations like Kapalua, Southern Utah at the Black Desert Resort and the Dominican Republic at Corales Puntacana.

The golf course is a Par 72 that measures close to 7,500 yards. I leaned heavily on Strokes Gained: Approach this week, along with Scrambling and Hole Proximity from 175 to 200+ yards. We got it done with Andrew Novak using a very similar formula last week, and I believe the puzzle is not all that different here. I also looked at Par 5 Scoring, Birdie or Better Percentage, 3-Putt Avoidance and Strokes Gained: Putting (Paspalum).

I already made reference to a few of the courses that I believe provide correlation: The Plantation Course at Kapalua, the former home of the Sentry Tournament of Champions, Corales, Vidanta Vallarta and Black Desert. I also believe there are connections with TPC Summerlin, the former home of the Shriners Children’s Open in Las Vegas, Sea Island (RSM Classic) and the Grand Reserve Golf Club, where they play the Puerto Rico Open.

I landed on Novak two weeks in a row and it worked, so let’s try again with the 19-year-old who was third earlier this season in Puerto Rico, 11th at Corales Puntacana and finished top-20 last week at Vidanta Vallarta – where off the tee he was brilliant, ranking eighth in Driving Distance and No. 1 in Driving Accuracy. Over the last 20 rounds, Brown ranks fifth in this field for SG: Approach and is 22nd in Scrambling.

Fisk is another player who can putt, is very good with the long irons and is both long and straight off the tee. He closed with a 63 last week at Vidanta to finish runner-up to Novak. A month ago, he finished seventh at Black Desert. This is only Fisk’s second full season on Tour, and he already has two wins. Last season he finished fourth in Puerto Rico. Over the last 20 rounds, he ranks third in this field for Hole Proximity from 175-200 yards.

It has been a minute since I have backed my fellow Las Vegas resident, but he seems to flourish in resort, coastal locations, with his last Tour victory coming at Port Royal Golf Club in Bermuda in 2022, where he just lost in a playoff two weeks ago. Power was 11th earlier this year at Corales Puntacana and has three top-10 finishes at Sea Island. Over the last 20 rounds, he ranks fifth in this field for Birdie or Better Percentage and is eighth in Scrambling.

Here’s a guy who has won at both Sea Island and Kapalua. Kirk has two top-10 finishes in his last three starts, and as noted earlier, he currently sits at 110th in the FedEx Cup standings. With the way he is playing, he looks on track to crack the top 100 very soon. Over the last 20 rounds, Kirk is No. 1 in this field for SG: Approach, No. 2 on the Par 5s, 11th in Scrambling and ninth in 3-Putt Avoidance.

Like Blades Brown, I’m going to give Clanton another go for the second week in a row. He is currently 123rd in the FedEx Cup Fall standings and has finished seventh, 11th and 29th in his last three starts. Clanton also finished fifth earlier this year in Puerto Rico and was runner-up at the 2024 RSM Classic. Over the last 20 rounds, he ranks sixth in this field for SG: Approach and is 17th for both Hole Proximity from 175-200 yards and in Scrambling. Clanton ranks 10th for SG: Par 5s and third for 3-Putt Avoidance.

McGreevy sits in a similar spot in the standings to Clanton and has also been playing well lately, with two top-30 finishes in two recent starts. He was 26th at Black Desert a month ago, where he ranked eighth in that field for SG: Off the Tee. He was 29th last week at Vidanta, where he ranked fourth in that field for SG: Approach. Over the last 20 rounds, McGreevy ranks fifth in this field for Hole Proximity from 175-200 yards and is 21st in Scrambling. McGreevy was 11th earlier this season in Puerto Rico. He finished runner-up at Corales Puntacana in 2022 and was runner-up last year at the RSM Classic. He finished 11th at Black Desert in both 2024 and in 2025.

extraction.body: Blades Brown has the game to win this week's World Wide Technology Championship Welcome to our weekly PGA Tour gambling-tips column, featuring picks from GOLF.com’s expert prognosticator, Brady Kannon. A seasoned golf bettor and commentator, Kannon is a host and regular guest on SportsGrid, a syndicated audio network devoted to sports and sports betting, and is a golf betting analyst for CBS Sportsline. You can follow Brady on Twitter at @LasVegasGolfer, and you can read his picks below for the 2026 World Wide Technology Championship, which gets underway on Thursday. In case you settled in for a brief siesta, no problemo, you haven’t missed anything. The PGA Tour remains in Mexico for the second straight week, shifting from Nuevo Vallarta, going northwest across the Gulf of California to Cabo San Lucas. It is the fourth edition of the World Wide Technology Championship to be held at the El Cardonal Course at the Diamante Resort, a Tiger Woods design, and it is the sixth of eight FedEx Cup Fall events in 2026. This is the first of the remaining three fall series tournaments for players to earn a spot in the top 100 of the FedExCup Standings and secure themselves a spot on Tour for the 2027 season. The RSM Classic at Sea Island in St. Simons Island, Georgia, is the final stop of the fall series, teeing off on Thursday, November 19. Here are those players currently ranked from 95-110 in the FedExCup Standings. (*denotes players who are exempt for 2027) 95. John Parry 96. Max Greyserman 97. Billy Horschel 98. Kevin Yu 99. Chandler Phillips 100. Jason Day 101. Mackenzie Hughes 102. Taylor Pendrith 103. Brandt Snedeker* 104. A.J. Ewart 105. Lee Hodges 106. Rasmus Neergaard-Petersen 107. Chandler Blanchet 108. Brooks Koepka* 109. Tony Finau* 110. Chris Kirk This golf course has proven to be one of the easier tracks on the Tour calendar. The average winning score over the first three times we have seen this course is nearly 27-under par. Ben Griffin is your defending champion, winning last fall with a score of 29-under. As at Vidanta Vallarta, El Cardonal’s main defense is the wind, given its location between the Gulf of California and the Pacific Ocean. However, the forecast looks tame, with high temperatures in the low 80s and light winds of 5-15 MPH. Also, like last week, the golf course is wall-to-wall Paspalum Grass with especially wide fairways and massive greens. For resort courses in windy locations, this design is not uncommon. It would be next to impossible for a typical resort guest to play a course in heavy winds without oversized fairways and greens. In addition, there is really no rough to speak of off the fairways at El Cardonal. Like these two Tour stops in Mexico, we see similar designs in potentially windy, resort locations like Kapalua, Southern Utah at the Black Desert Resort and the Dominican Republic at Corales Puntacana. The golf course is a Par 72 that measures close to 7,500 yards. I leaned heavily on Strokes Gained: Approach this week, along with Scrambling and Hole Proximity from 175 to 200+ yards. We got it done with Andrew Novak using a very similar formula last week, and I believe the puzzle is not all that different here. I also looked at Par 5 Scoring, Birdie or Better Percentage, 3-Putt Avoidance and Strokes Gained: Putting (Paspalum). I already made reference to a few of the courses that I believe provide correlation: The Plantation Course at Kapalua, the former home of the Sentry Tournament of Champions, Corales, Vidanta Vallarta and Black Desert. I also believe there are connections with TPC Summerlin, the former home of the Shriners Children’s Open in Las Vegas, Sea Island (RSM Classic) and the Grand Reserve Golf Club, where they play the Puerto Rico Open. I landed on Novak two weeks in a row and it worked, so let’s try again with the 19-year-old who was third earlier this season in Puerto Rico, 11th at Corales Puntacana and finished top-20 last week at Vidanta Vallarta – where off the tee he was brilliant, ranking eighth in Driving Distance and No. 1 in Driving Accuracy. Over the last 20 rounds, Brown ranks fifth in this field for SG: Approach and is 22nd in Scrambling. Fisk is another player who can putt, is very good with the long irons and is both long and straight off the tee. He closed with a 63 last week at Vidanta to finish runner-up to Novak. A month ago, he finished seventh at Black Desert. This is only Fisk’s second full season on Tour, and he already has two wins. Last season he finished fourth in Puerto Rico. Over the last 20 rounds, he ranks third in this field for Hole Proximity from 175-200 yards. It has been a minute since I have backed my fellow Las Vegas resident, but he seems to flourish in resort, coastal locations, with his last Tour victory coming at Port Royal Golf Club in Bermuda in 2022, where he just lost in a playoff two weeks ago. Power was 11th earlier this year at Corales Puntacana and has three top-10 finishes at Sea Island. Over the last 20 rounds, he ranks fifth in this field for Birdie or Better Percentage and is eighth in Scrambling. Here’s a guy who has won at both Sea Island and Kapalua. Kirk has two top-10 finishes in his last three starts, and as noted earlier, he currently sits at 110th in the FedEx Cup standings. With the way he is playing, he looks on track to crack the top 100 very soon. Over the last 20 rounds, Kirk is No. 1 in this field for SG: Approach, No. 2 on the Par 5s, 11th in Scrambling and ninth in 3-Putt Avoidance. Like Blades Brown, I’m going to give Clanton another go for the second week in a row. He is currently 123rd in the FedEx Cup Fall standings and has finished seventh, 11th and 29th in his last three starts. Clanton also finished fifth earlier this year in Puerto Rico and was runner-up at the 2024 RSM Classic. Over the last 20 rounds, he ranks sixth in this field for SG: Approach and is 17th for both Hole Proximity from 175-200 yards and in Scrambling. Clanton ranks 10th for SG: Par 5s and third for 3-Putt Avoidance. McGreevy sits in a similar spot in the standings to Clanton and has also been playing well lately, with two top-30 finishes in two recent starts. He was 26th at Black Desert a month ago, where he ranked eighth in that field for SG: Off the Tee. He was 29th last week at Vidanta, where he ranked fourth in that field for SG: Approach. Over the last 20 rounds, McGreevy ranks fifth in this field for Hole Proximity from 175-200 yards and is 21st in Scrambling. McGreevy was 11th earlier this season in Puerto Rico. He finished runner-up at Corales Puntacana in 2022 and was runner-up last year at the RSM Classic. He finished 11th at Black Desert in both 2024 and in 2025. sources.title: Binance co-CEO Richard Teng says hackers used fake job interviews, AI tool to steal $6.3 billion in crypto - CNBC
passages: Binance said hackers used fake job interviews, malicious software and compromised internal AI tools to infiltrate its wallet infrastructure, leading to the record-breaking Oct.
29 cyberattack that resulted in more than $6 billion in assets being stolen from the world's largest crypto exchange.

The attackers "spent months building their way in," Binance co-CEO Richard Teng told CNBC's " Squawk on the Street " Tuesday, rejecting suggestions that there was a single point of failure through one employee's laptop.
As Binance works to recover from the incident, it has temporarily restricted certain withdrawals, pledged to cover all customer losses and tapped its own reserves to replenish affected assets.
Coinbase blocked transfers to compromised wallets and offered Binance direct assistance.
He also said Binance has replenished 98% of $6.34 billion in affected assets, and that it is still in the process of purchasing outstanding, more illiquid assets.
"In June, [the attackers] set up a fake version of a developer tool and lured one of our engineers to install that," he added.
The hack sparked a sharp but short-lived hit to confidence across crypto markets, especially compared with previous failures at major exchanges.
Investors are now watching whether Binance can fully restore confidence in centralized exchanges.

Although the incident represents a significant security breach, Binance maintains that it remains financially sound and focused on identifying the vulnerability, recovering remaining funds and preventing another attack.
Teng himself did not attribute the attack to North Korea but acknowledged that the FBI has linked it to North Korean hackers tied to the TraderTraitor group.

extraction.body: Binance said hackers used fake job interviews, malicious software and compromised internal AI tools to infiltrate its wallet infrastructure, leading to the record-breaking Oct. 29 cyberattack that resulted in more than $6 billion in assets being stolen from the world's largest crypto exchange. The attackers "spent months building their way in," Binance co-CEO Richard Teng told CNBC's " Squawk on the Street " Tuesday, rejecting suggestions that there was a single point of failure through one employee's laptop. "In June, [the attackers] set up a fake version of a developer tool and lured one of our engineers to install that," he added. "In September they posed as recruiters and ran a series of job interviews with another engineer, and that ended up in a coding exercise that contained hidden malware designed to evade security ... from there they moved violently through our internal AI tools and obtain[ed] access that breach[ed] the system that authorized our wallet transaction." He also said Binance has replenished 98% of $6.34 billion in affected assets, and that it is still in the process of purchasing outstanding, more illiquid assets. Teng himself did not attribute the attack to North Korea but acknowledged that the FBI has linked it to North Korean hackers tied to the TraderTraitor group. Preparations for the attack began in June, when a Binance Wallet DevOps engineer downloaded a tampered Homebrew installation "to install a popular AI coding tool after searching for it on a search engine," according to a security report published by Binance Tuesday. It said it detected the suspicious activity, replaced the engineer's device and rotated credentials as a precaution, but that by then the employee's "role and his related colleagues on our wallet infrastructure team was exposed to the hacker." As Binance works to recover from the incident, it has temporarily restricted certain withdrawals, pledged to cover all customer losses and tapped its own reserves to replenish affected assets. Binance and industry partners including Tether, Circle and Ripple have reportedly frozen about $3 billion in assets, though some stolen funds continue to move through laundered channels. Coinbase blocked transfers to compromised wallets and offered Binance direct assistance. Although the incident represents a significant security breach, Binance maintains that it remains financially sound and focused on identifying the vulnerability, recovering remaining funds and preventing another attack. The hack sparked a sharp but short-lived hit to confidence across crypto markets, especially compared with previous failures at major exchanges. Investors are now watching whether Binance can fully restore confidence in centralized exchanges. As of Tuesday Binance has rebuilt the affected wallet system and internal AI tool, replaced compromised devices, decommissioned credentials and tokens associated with the affected engineers and expanded security scans across employee devices, Teng told "Squawk on the Street." "We're also getting an independent expert to review everything that we have done, and we'll keep strengthening our defenses as the investigation continues," Teng said. Teng himself did not attribute the attack to North Korea but acknowledged that the FBI has linked it to North Korean hackers tied to the TraderTraitor group.

Although the incident represents a significant security breach, Binance maintains that it remains financially sound and focused on identifying the vulnerability, recovering remaining funds and preventing another attack.

The hack sparked a sharp but short-lived hit to confidence across crypto markets, especially compared with previous failures at major exchanges. Investors are now watching whether Binance can fully restore confidence in centralized exchanges.

As of Tuesday Binance has rebuilt the affected wallet system and internal AI tool, replaced compromised devices, decommissioned credentials and tokens associated with the affected engineers and expanded security scans across employee devices, Teng told "Squawk on the Street."

"We're also getting an independent expert to review everything that we have done, and we'll keep strengthening our defenses as the investigation continues," Teng said. "We're working around the clock with law enforcement agencies and with industry partners to trace and freeze the stolen funds for that front."

The attackers "spent months building their way in," Binance co-CEO Richard Teng told CNBC's " Squawk on the Street " Tuesday, rejecting suggestions that there was a single point of failure through one employee's laptop.

"In June, [the attackers] set up a fake version of a developer tool and lured one of our engineers to install that," he added. "In September they posed as recruiters and ran a series of job interviews with another engineer, and that ended up in a coding exercise that contained hidden malware designed to evade security ... from there they moved violently through our internal AI tools and obtain[ed] access that breach[ed] the system that authorized our wallet transaction."
He also said Binance has replenished 98% of $6.34 billion in affected assets, and that it is still in the process of purchasing outstanding, more illiquid assets.
Teng himself did not attribute the attack to North Korea but acknowledged that the FBI has linked it to North Korean hackers tied to the TraderTraitor group.

Preparations for the attack began in June, when a Binance Wallet DevOps engineer downloaded a tampered Homebrew installation "to install a popular AI coding tool after searching for it on a search engine," according to a security report published by Binance Tuesday. It said it detected the suspicious activity, replaced the engineer's device and rotated credentials as a precaution, but that by then the employee's "role and his related colleagues on our wallet infrastructure team was exposed to the hacker."

As Binance works to recover from the incident, it has temporarily restricted certain withdrawals, pledged to cover all customer losses and tapped its own reserves to replenish affected assets. Binance and industry partners including Tether, Circle and Ripple have reportedly frozen about $3 billion in assets, though some stolen funds continue to move through laundered channels. Coinbase blocked transfers to compromised wallets and offered Binance direct assistance.

Although the incident represents a significant security breach, Binance maintains that it remains financially sound and focused on identifying the vulnerability, recovering remaining funds and preventing another attack.

The hack sparked a sharp but short-lived hit to confidence across crypto markets, especially compared with previous failures at major exchanges. Investors are now watching whether Binance can fully restore confidence in centralized exchanges.

As of Tuesday Binance has rebuilt the affected wallet system and internal AI tool, replaced compromised devices, decommissioned credentials and tokens associated with the affected engineers and expanded security scans across employee devices, Teng told "Squawk on the Street."

"We're also getting an independent expert to review everything that we have done, and we'll keep strengthening our defenses as the investigation continues," Teng said. "We're working around the clock with law enforcement agencies and with industry partners to trace and freeze the stolen funds for that front."

passages: It has been a busy few days for Changpeng Zhao in the wake of the hack on the enormous crypto platform he co-founded, Binance.
"It's been a pretty hectic process," Zhao, better known in crypto circles as CZ , told Yahoo Finance.
"But the good thing is right now the withdrawals have been restored, the systems back to normal.
People are free to use the platform without any issues now.
"So when you run a platform, especially a crypto platform the possibility is always there.
I did not think it was going to be this big of magnitude, probably not."
Hackers recently drained roughly $6.3 billion worth of digital assets from Binance on Oct.
Binance is the world's largest cryptocurrency trading platform and holds approximately $171 billion in total assets on its platform.
The company is led by co-CEOs Richard Teng and Yi Le.
Rather than cracking private cryptographic keys, the attackers reportedly breached internal automated transaction workflows via a Binance employee's laptop.

Binance moved swiftly to stabilize the situation by guaranteeing full customer restitution, deploying corporate treasury reserves, Secure Asset Fund for Users (SAFU) capital, and insurance funds to replenish user balances.

He also warned that artificial intelligence could make similar attacks increasingly common, potentially exposing weaknesses throughout the financial system. The October 29 attack took approximately 20 minutes, with hackers draining an estimated $6.3 billion from Binance wallets. Blockchain intelligence firms and the FBI have attributed the theft with high confidence to TraderTraitor, a North Korean state-sponsored hacking group, although North Korea has denied involvement. The attackers reportedly compromised a Binance employee's laptop and exploited internal automated transaction systems rather than breaking the cryptographic keys protecting customer assets. The distinction is particularly troubling because it suggests that sophisticated blockchain security can be circumvented through comparatively familiar weaknesses in the institutions operating the technology. Binance temporarily suspended withdrawals while attempting to contain the attack and trace the stolen assets. Zhao said withdrawals have since resumed and the platform is operating normally, with customers protected from financial losses. "The users did not suffer any loss," Zhao told Yahoo Finance, explaining that Binance itself had absorbed the financial impact. The exchange has drawn on corporate reserves, insurance funds and its Secure Asset Fund for Users to replenish affected balances. That commitment is substantial even for a platform holding approximately $171 billion in assets. Binance reported that it had secured coverage for 90% of the affected assets by October 31, with additional purchases underway to replace less liquid cryptocurrencies. Zhao, who stepped down as Binance CEO in 2023, said he learned of the attack almost simultaneously through social media and internal communications. Although he no longer manages the company, he used his public presence and position as a shareholder to reassure customers that their balances would be protected. His assessment of the broader threat was considerably less reassuring. Zhao believes artificial intelligence is giving attackers powerful new tools to discover vulnerabilities faster than financial institutions can defend against them. In the accompanying Yahoo Finance interview, he argued that AI can analyze code, identify bugs and examine systems at a scale previously difficult for human attackers. Defensive applications, in his view, have not advanced at the same pace, creating an increasingly dangerous imbalance between those attempting to penetrate financial systems and those responsible for protecting them. The concern extends beyond cryptocurrency exchanges. Banks, custodians and other financial institutions depend on interconnected software, employee access controls and automated processes that may be vulnerable even when their underlying transaction systems remain secure. Binance's experience also exposes a distinction between protecting customer balances and preventing institutional losses. The exchange's financial resources allowed it to promise restitution after an extraordinary theft, but smaller platforms might not have sufficient capital to make the same commitment. The speed of the response demonstrated another unusual feature of digital-asset markets. Stablecoin issuers and blockchain investigators were able to identify and freeze billions of dollars associated with the attack, although substantial amounts were moved into assets that could not be frozen through the same mechanisms. Those interventions helped limit the damage, but they also revealed how much the cryptocurrency market now depends on centralized institutions capable of intervening when decentralized transactions go wrong. The same industry built around the promise of reducing reliance on financial intermediaries increasingly needs those intermediaries to protect its customers. Zhao's warning arrives as digital assets continue moving into mainstream investment portfolios and financial platforms. The question of custody is becoming inseparable from the financial strength, operational discipline and technological defenses of the institutions holding those assets. Binance appears capable of surviving an attack that would overwhelm many financial businesses. Yet Zhao's most consequential observation was not about the money his company could replace, but about the possibility that increasingly sophisticated attacks will become harder to prevent. The comment landed in the middle of a leading cybersecurity story, and it came paired with a reassurance. Zhao said withdrawals had been restored and systems were back to normal. He also said he had not expected the Binance hack to reach “this big of magnitude.” Beyond that, he told users that “All user funds are covered” and that “The users did not suffer any loss.” Those two sentences matter as much as the headline quote, because they shape whether customers keep their money on the platform. This analysis separates what outlets have confirmed from what remains open. It looks at what Zhao actually said, what the claims mean for exchange customers, and where the story could go next. For background on one reported intrusion route, see our earlier look at the reported attack chain . Here, the focus stays on the statements, the market reaction and the security lessons. Zhao made three separate points in the coverage so far. First, he acknowledged that no platform can promise perfect protection. Second, he said the scale of the incident surprised him. Third, he told users that operations had returned to normal and that nobody lost money. The tone is worth noting. Founders of large exchanges usually avoid saying a breach was possible, let alone expected. Zhao did the opposite. He framed the incident as a risk that comes with running any crypto platform, which is an honest position and also a convenient one. It lowers the bar for what customers should expect from Binance while still asking them to trust the cover story on funds. What did Zhao leave out? He gave no technical cause, no timeline of the intrusion and no breakdown of how the cover for users is funded, at least in the coverage we reviewed. Those gaps are normal in the first week of an investigation, but they define what readers can and cannot conclude today. A statement of principle fills the silence until facts arrive. Yahoo Finance, CoinDesk and Global Finance Magazine all carried the story in the days after the hack. Everything in this piece that carries quotation marks comes from a small set of confirmed statements. Where a detail circulated online without confirmation, we say so. coreStoryFacts.text: It has been a busy few days for Changpeng Zhao in the wake of the hack on the enormous crypto platform he co-founded, Binance.
"It's been a pretty hectic process," Zhao, better known in crypto circles as CZ , told Yahoo Finance.
"But the good thing is right now the withdrawals have been restored, the systems back to normal.
People are free to use the platform without any issues now.
"So when you run a platform, especially a crypto platform the possibility is always there.
I did not think it was going to be this big of magnitude, probably not."
Hackers recently drained roughly $6.3 billion worth of digital assets from Binance on Oct.
Binance is the world's largest cryptocurrency trading platform and holds approximately $171 billion in total assets on its platform.
The company is led by co-CEOs Richard Teng and Yi Le.
Rather than cracking private cryptographic keys, the attackers reportedly breached internal automated transaction workflows via a Binance employee's laptop.

Binance moved swiftly to stabilize the situation by guaranteeing full customer restitution, deploying corporate treasury reserves, Secure Asset Fund for Users (SAFU) capital, and insurance funds to replenish user balances.
Changpeng Zhao never expected hackers to steal $6.3 billion from Binance, the cryptocurrency exchange he founded.
But after the largest crypto heist in history, his response was remarkably matter-of-fact: “There's no 100% security.”
Blockchain intelligence firms and the FBI have attributed the theft with high confidence to TraderTraitor, a North Korean state-sponsored hacking group, although North Korea has denied involvement.
That commitment is substantial even for a platform holding approximately $171 billion in assets.

News, research and resources for financial advisors and wealth management professionals.

Speaking with Yahoo Finance's Brian Sozzi on Tuesday, Zhao acknowledged that a breach of this magnitude had seemed unlikely even as Binance grew into the world's largest cryptocurrency trading platform.
"The users did not suffer any loss," Zhao told Yahoo Finance, explaining that Binance itself had absorbed the financial impact.
Zhao, who stepped down as Binance CEO in 2023, said he learned of the attack almost simultaneously through social media and internal communications.

facts.text: It has been a busy few days for Changpeng Zhao in the wake of the hack on the enormous crypto platform he co-founded, Binance.
"It's been a pretty hectic process," Zhao, better known in crypto circles as CZ , told Yahoo Finance.
"But the good thing is right now the withdrawals have been restored, the systems back to normal.
People are free to use the platform without any issues now.
"So when you run a platform, especially a crypto platform the possibility is always there.
I did not think it was going to be this big of magnitude, probably not."
Hackers recently drained roughly $6.3 billion worth of digital assets from Binance on Oct.
Binance is the world's largest cryptocurrency trading platform and holds approximately $171 billion in total assets on its platform.
The company is led by co-CEOs Richard Teng and Yi Le.
Rather than cracking private cryptographic keys, the attackers reportedly breached internal automated transaction workflows via a Binance employee's laptop.

Binance moved swiftly to stabilize the situation by guaranteeing full customer restitution, deploying corporate treasury reserves, Secure Asset Fund for Users (SAFU) capital, and insurance funds to replenish user balances.
Changpeng Zhao never expected hackers to steal $6.3 billion from Binance, the cryptocurrency exchange he founded.
But after the largest crypto heist in history, his response was remarkably matter-of-fact: “There's no 100% security.”
Blockchain intelligence firms and the FBI have attributed the theft with high confidence to TraderTraitor, a North Korean state-sponsored hacking group, although North Korea has denied involvement.
That commitment is substantial even for a platform holding approximately $171 billion in assets.

Zhao, who stepped down as Binance CEO in 2023, said he learned of the attack almost simultaneously through social media and internal communications.

The comment landed in the middle of a leading cybersecurity story, and it came paired with a reassurance.
Zhao said withdrawals had been restored and systems were back to normal.
That may reflect an active investigation, where lawyers and agencies limit what a company can say.
It may also reflect that the facts are still being established.

The coverage we reviewed includes none of those numbers for this incident.

Changpeng Zhao never expected hackers to steal $6.3 billion from Binance, the cryptocurrency exchange he founded. But after the largest crypto heist in history, his response was remarkably matter-of-fact: “There's no 100% security.” Speaking with Yahoo Finance's Brian Sozzi on Tuesday, Zhao acknowledged that a breach of this magnitude had seemed unlikely even as Binance grew into the world's largest cryptocurrency trading platform. He also warned that artificial intelligence could make similar attacks increasingly common, potentially exposing weaknesses throughout the financial system. The October 29 attack took approximately 20 minutes, with hackers draining an estimated $6.3 billion from Binance wallets. Blockchain intelligence firms and the FBI have attributed the theft with high confidence to TraderTraitor, a North Korean state-sponsored hacking group, although North Korea has denied involvement. The attackers reportedly compromised a Binance employee's laptop and exploited internal automated transaction systems rather than breaking the cryptographic keys protecting customer assets. The distinction is particularly troubling because it suggests that sophisticated blockchain security can be circumvented through comparatively familiar weaknesses in the institutions operating the technology. Binance temporarily suspended withdrawals while attempting to contain the attack and trace the stolen assets. Zhao said withdrawals have since resumed and the platform is operating normally, with customers protected from financial losses. "The users did not suffer any loss," Zhao told Yahoo Finance, explaining that Binance itself had absorbed the financial impact. The exchange has drawn on corporate reserves, insurance funds and its Secure Asset Fund for Users to replenish affected balances. That commitment is substantial even for a platform holding approximately $171 billion in assets. Binance reported that it had secured coverage for 90% of the affected assets by October 31, with additional purchases underway to replace less liquid cryptocurrencies. Zhao, who stepped down as Binance CEO in 2023, said he learned of the attack almost simultaneously through social media and internal communications. Although he no longer manages the company, he used his public presence and position as a shareholder to reassure customers that their balances would be protected. His assessment of the broader threat was considerably less reassuring. Zhao believes artificial intelligence is giving attackers powerful new tools to discover vulnerabilities faster than financial institutions can defend against them. In the accompanying Yahoo Finance interview, he argued that AI can analyze code, identify bugs and examine systems at a scale previously difficult for human attackers. Defensive applications, in his view, have not advanced at the same pace, creating an increasingly dangerous imbalance between those attempting to penetrate financial systems and those responsible for protecting them. The concern extends beyond cryptocurrency exchanges. Banks, custodians and other financial institutions depend on interconnected software, employee access controls and automated processes that may be vulnerable even when their underlying transaction systems remain secure. Binance's experience also exposes a distinction between protecting customer balances and preventing institutional losses. The exchange's financial resources allowed it to promise restitution after an extraordinary theft, but smaller platforms might not have sufficient capital to make the same commitment. The speed of the response demonstrated another unusual feature of digital-asset markets. Stablecoin issuers and blockchain investigators were able to identify and freeze billions of dollars associated with the attack, although substantial amounts were moved into assets that could not be frozen through the same mechanisms. Those interventions helped limit the damage, but they also revealed how much the cryptocurrency market now depends on centralized institutions capable of intervening when decentralized transactions go wrong. The same industry built around the promise of reducing reliance on financial intermediaries increasingly needs those intermediaries to protect its customers. Zhao's warning arrives as digital assets continue moving into mainstream investment portfolios and financial platforms. The question of custody is becoming inseparable from the financial strength, operational discipline and technological defenses of the institutions holding those assets. Binance appears capable of surviving an attack that would overwhelm many financial businesses. Yet Zhao's most consequential observation was not about the money his company could replace, but about the possibility that increasingly sophisticated attacks will become harder to prevent. The world's largest cryptocurrency exchange has demonstrated that it can make customers whole after losing billions of dollars. It has not demonstrated that the next attack can be stopped. extraction.body: Binance founder Changpeng Zhao, widely known as CZ, said “There’s no 100% security” after hackers drained roughly $6.3 billion in digital assets from the exchange on October 29, 2026, according to Yahoo Finance . The comment landed in the middle of a leading cybersecurity story, and it came paired with a reassurance. Zhao said withdrawals had been restored and systems were back to normal. He also said he had not expected the Binance hack to reach “this big of magnitude.” Beyond that, he told users that “All user funds are covered” and that “The users did not suffer any loss.” Those two sentences matter as much as the headline quote, because they shape whether customers keep their money on the platform. This analysis separates what outlets have confirmed from what remains open. It looks at what Zhao actually said, what the claims mean for exchange customers, and where the story could go next. For background on one reported intrusion route, see our earlier look at the reported attack chain . Here, the focus stays on the statements, the market reaction and the security lessons. Zhao made three separate points in the coverage so far. First, he acknowledged that no platform can promise perfect protection. Second, he said the scale of the incident surprised him. Third, he told users that operations had returned to normal and that nobody lost money. The tone is worth noting. Founders of large exchanges usually avoid saying a breach was possible, let alone expected. Zhao did the opposite. He framed the incident as a risk that comes with running any crypto platform, which is an honest position and also a convenient one. It lowers the bar for what customers should expect from Binance while still asking them to trust the cover story on funds. What did Zhao leave out? He gave no technical cause, no timeline of the intrusion and no breakdown of how the cover for users is funded, at least in the coverage we reviewed. Those gaps are normal in the first week of an investigation, but they define what readers can and cannot conclude today. A statement of principle fills the silence until facts arrive. Yahoo Finance, CoinDesk and Global Finance Magazine all carried the story in the days after the hack. Everything in this piece that carries quotation marks comes from a small set of confirmed statements. Where a detail circulated online without confirmation, we say so. The table below sorts the core claims into what outlets confirmed and what they did not. We kept it deliberately narrow. A short list of firm facts beats a long list of shaky ones. As a statement of engineering fact, Zhao is right. Every security team in every industry works from the same premise: you reduce risk, you do not remove it. Banks, cloud providers and exchanges all accept residual risk and buy insurance against it. The WealthAdvisor framed his remarks as a warning that no crypto platform is completely safe. Zhao went further in the Yahoo Finance coverage. He said that when you run a platform, “especially a crypto platform the possibility is always there.” That sentence is the most useful one in the whole story, because it shifts the conversation from blame to risk management. A platform that handles billions in customer assets becomes a target by definition. Still, the statement is incomplete as a customer message. “No 100% security” says nothing about where the other 1% of risk sits, who bears it, or how fast the platform finds problems. Security leaders usually answer those questions with detection time, blast radius and recovery plans. The coverage we reviewed includes none of those numbers for this incident. That gap explains why the quote spread so quickly. It is short, honest and quotable. It also leaves every hard question unanswered. Zhao told the outlet he “did not think it was going to be this big of magnitude, probably not.” For a founder who built one of the largest exchanges in the world, that admission cuts two ways. It signals humility. It also signals that risk models inside the industry may have underestimated the worst case. A $6.3 billion loss is not a normal operating incident. At that scale, a company cannot absorb the hit through routine insurance claims or a quick top-up. It needs balance-sheet depth, regulator contact and a communication plan on the first day. The fact that Zhao says users were made whole suggests Binance had that depth, though the outlets we cite do not detail how the cover was funded. sources.title: Thousands of Android apps can track your phone — even if you deny permissions
passages: There are fixes coming for some of these issues in Android Q, according to the researchers, who say they notified Google about the vulnerabilities last September. (They point to this official Google page.) Yet, that may not help the many current-generation Android phones that won’t get the Android Q update. (As of May, only 10.4 percent of Android devices had the latest Android P installed, and over 60 percent were still running on the nearly three-year-old Android N.) The researchers think that Google should do more, possibly rolling out hotfixes within security updates in the meantime because it shouldn’t just be newer phone buyers who get protection. “Google is publicly claiming that privacy should not be a luxury good, but that very well appears to be what’s happening here,” said Egelman.

But researchers say that thousands of apps have found ways to cheat Android’s permissions system, phoning home your device’s unique identifier and enough data to potentially reveal your location as well.

The study also singles out photo app Shutterfly for sending actual GPS coordinates back to its servers without getting permission to track locations — by harvesting that data from your photos’ EXIF metadata — though the company denied that it gathers that data without permission in a statement to CNET.

extraction.body: When you explicitly tell an Android app, “No, you don’t have permission to track my phone,” you probably expect that it won’t have abilities that let it do that. But researchers say that thousands of apps have found ways to cheat Android’s permissions system, phoning home your device’s unique identifier and enough data to potentially reveal your location as well. Even if you say “no” to one app when it asks for permission to see those personally identifying bits of data, it might not be enough: a second app with permissions you have approved can share those bits with the other one or leave them in shared storage where another app — potentially even a malicious one — can read it. The two apps might not seem related, but researchers say that because they’re built using the same software development kits (SDK), they can access that data, and there’s evidence that the SDK owners are receiving it. It’s like a kid asking for dessert who gets told “no” by one parent, so they ask the other parent. According to a study presented at PrivacyCon 2019, we’re talking about apps from the likes of Samsung and Disney that have been downloaded hundreds of millions of times. They use SDKs built by Chinese search giant Baidu and an analytics firm called Salmonads that could pass your data from one app to another (and to their servers) by storing it locally on your phone first. Researchers saw that some apps using the Baidu SDK may be attempting to quietly obtain this data for their own use. That’s in addition to a number of side channel vulnerabilities the team found, some of which can send home the unique MAC addresses of your networking chip and router, wireless access point, its SSID, and more. “It’s pretty well-known now that’s a pretty good surrogate for location data,” said Serge Egelman, research director of the Usable Security and Privacy Group at the International Computer Science Institute (ICSI), when presenting the study at PrivacyCon. The study also singles out photo app Shutterfly for sending actual GPS coordinates back to its servers without getting permission to track locations — by harvesting that data from your photos’ EXIF metadata — though the company denied that it gathers that data without permission in a statement to CNET. There are fixes coming for some of these issues in Android Q, according to the researchers, who say they notified Google about the vulnerabilities last September. (They point to this official Google page.) Yet, that may not help the many current-generation Android phones that won’t get the Android Q update. (As of May, only 10.4 percent of Android devices had the latest Android P installed, and over 60 percent were still running on the nearly three-year-old Android N.) The researchers think that Google should do more, possibly rolling out hotfixes within security updates in the meantime because it shouldn’t just be newer phone buyers who get protection. “Google is publicly claiming that privacy should not be a luxury good, but that very well appears to be what’s happening here,” said Egelman. Google declined to comment on the specific vulnerabilities, but it confirmed to The Verge that Android Q will hide geolocation info from photo apps by default, and it will require photo apps to tell the Play Store whether they’re capable of accessing location metadata.

extraction.body: Staying on top of what information your apps can access is always a good idea. It's great that we have access to hundreds of thousands of apps on our smartphones, but it's always worth being mindful of which apps you install. Though Android and iOS have surprisingly effective built-in security measures to detect and block malicious apps, some apps may still pose a risk if they have access to sensitive information or device features. An app requesting permission to access your camera, location, text messages or files doesn't necessarily mean it's unsafe, but it's worth asking why it needs them in the first place — especially if they have little to do with what the app is actually supposed to do. Reviewing app permissions on your phone every once in a while is therefore a good way to keep your personal data secure, and thankfully, both Android and iOS let you do so fairly easily through their settings menus. If you don't want an app to access your location in the background, for instance, you can revoke that permission or change it so the app can only access your location when you're actively using it. Your device's camera and location details are especially sensitive, which is why Android and iOS show on-screen indicators when an app is actively using your camera, microphone or accessing location. The iPhone displays a green dot when your camera is in use, an orange dot when an app is listening via the microphone and a blue location icon when an app pings your whereabouts. Android phones use similar status bar icons, and you can swipe down to access the Control Center or the quick settings panel to see which app is accessing these features. Apple is known for being privacy-oriented, so it's no surprise that its operating systems have sophisticated privacy and security measures. Both iOS 27 and iPadOS 27 handle app permissions similarly. Any third-party app you install and use for the first time is required to request your permission before it can access information like your contacts, photos, location or microphone. When an app requests location access, you can tap Allow Once if you want to grant it temporarily, or select Allow While Using App if you trust the service. You can also view and manage app permissions at any time by navigating to Settings > Privacy & Security . This section lists each permission type alongside the number of apps accessing it. For instance, tapping Microphone shows every app on your phone allowed to access it. You can revoke access for any app by turning the toggle off next to its name. Certain apps like Google Maps or Uber might work optimally only if you've granted them the Precise Location permission and have set their location access to Always . You can dial these permissions back on a per-app basis, too. Similarly, when an app requests access to your camera roll, you can set the permission type to Limited Access and select only the photos and videos you want to share. If you enable App Privacy Report , you can view which apps have accessed your phone's data and sensors. This section also lets you monitor the network activity for apps so you can see which domains they're contacting and when. Android's privacy features have improved considerably over the years, and like iOS, you can view and manage permissions on a per-app basis. While the exact menu labels will vary depending on the manufacturer, you should be able to find detailed information on which apps have access to your camera, microphone, location, contacts and other data very easily. The easiest way to revoke a specific app's permissions is to open its App info page. You can get there by long-tapping the app's icon and selecting the i icon. Alternatively, navigate to Settings > Apps > See all apps and select the app from the list. Tap on Permissions , select a data type and choose Allow or Don't allow . Some device permissions, like location, let you set the access type to All the time or Allow only while using the app . Android also offers the Privacy dashboard , which lets you view different permission types and which apps have accessed them in the past 24 hours. Once again, the exact steps to get to this menu will vary. Try looking for this feature in the Security and privacy submenu in the Settings app, or type it into the search box. Android apps must ask for device permissions when you first launch them, and you can either allow or deny these requests. Both the Play Store and the App Store also list what information an app may request access to, giving you another way to review permissions before installing it.

You can also view and manage app permissions at any time by navigating to Settings > Privacy & Security . This section lists each permission type alongside the number of apps accessing it. For instance, tapping Microphone shows every app on your phone allowed to access it. You can revoke access for any app by turning the toggle off next to its name.

Certain apps like Google Maps or Uber might work optimally only if you've granted them the Precise Location permission and have set their location access to Always . You can dial these permissions back on a per-app basis, too. Similarly, when an app requests access to your camera roll, you can set the permission type to Limited Access and select only the photos and videos you want to share.

If you enable App Privacy Report , you can view which apps have accessed your phone's data and sensors. This section also lets you monitor the network activity for apps so you can see which domains they're contacting and when.

Android's privacy features have improved considerably over the years, and like iOS, you can view and manage permissions on a per-app basis. While the exact menu labels will vary depending on the manufacturer, you should be able to find detailed information on which apps have access to your camera, microphone, location, contacts and other data very easily.

The easiest way to revoke a specific app's permissions is to open its App info page. You can get there by long-tapping the app's icon and selecting the i icon. Alternatively, navigate to Settings > Apps > See all apps and select the app from the list. Tap on Permissions , select a data type and choose Allow or Don't allow . Some device permissions, like location, let you set the access type to All the time or Allow only while using the app .

Android also offers the Privacy dashboard , which lets you view different permission types and which apps have accessed them in the past 24 hours. Once again, the exact steps to get to this menu will vary. Try looking for this feature in the Security and privacy submenu in the Settings app, or type it into the search box.

Android apps must ask for device permissions when you first launch them, and you can either allow or deny these requests. Both the Play Store and the App Store also list what information an app may request access to, giving you another way to review permissions before installing it.
