extraction.body: When you explicitly tell an Android app, “No, you don’t have permission to track my phone,” you probably expect that it won’t have abilities that let it do that. But researchers say that thousands of apps have found ways to cheat Android’s permissions system, phoning home your device’s unique identifier and enough data to potentially reveal your location as well. Even if you say “no” to one app when it asks for permission to see those personally identifying bits of data, it might not be enough: a second app with permissions you have approved can share those bits with the other one or leave them in shared storage where another app — potentially even a malicious one — can read it. The two apps might not seem related, but researchers say that because they’re built using the same software development kits (SDK), they can access that data, and there’s evidence that the SDK owners are receiving it. It’s like a kid asking for dessert who gets told “no” by one parent, so they ask the other parent. According to a study presented at PrivacyCon 2019, we’re talking about apps from the likes of Samsung and Disney that have been downloaded hundreds of millions of times. They use SDKs built by Chinese search giant Baidu and an analytics firm called Salmonads that could pass your data from one app to another (and to their servers) by storing it locally on your phone first. Researchers saw that some apps using the Baidu SDK may be attempting to quietly obtain this data for their own use. That’s in addition to a number of side channel vulnerabilities the team found, some of which can send home the unique MAC addresses of your networking chip and router, wireless access point, its SSID, and more. “It’s pretty well-known now that’s a pretty good surrogate for location data,” said Serge Egelman, research director of the Usable Security and Privacy Group at the International Computer Science Institute (ICSI), when presenting the study at PrivacyCon. The study also singles out photo app Shutterfly for sending actual GPS coordinates back to its servers without getting permission to track locations — by harvesting that data from your photos’ EXIF metadata — though the company denied that it gathers that data without permission in a statement to CNET. There are fixes coming for some of these issues in Android Q, according to the researchers, who say they notified Google about the vulnerabilities last September. (They point to this official Google page.) Yet, that may not help the many current-generation Android phones that won’t get the Android Q update. (As of May, only 10.4 percent of Android devices had the latest Android P installed, and over 60 percent were still running on the nearly three-year-old Android N.) The researchers think that Google should do more, possibly rolling out hotfixes within security updates in the meantime because it shouldn’t just be newer phone buyers who get protection. “Google is publicly claiming that privacy should not be a luxury good, but that very well appears to be what’s happening here,” said Egelman. Google declined to comment on the specific vulnerabilities, but it confirmed to The Verge that Android Q will hide geolocation info from photo apps by default, and it will require photo apps to tell the Play Store whether they’re capable of accessing location metadata.

passages: NORWELL, Mass. and MIAMI , March 12, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- The National Organization for Rare Disorders (NORD ® ) and OpenEvidence today announced a new partnership to expand access to trusted, expert-reviewed rare disease information for clinicians, patients and families.

In partnership with more than 350 disease-specific member patient organizations and 46 NORD Rare Disease Centers of Excellence, NORD advances care, research, education and advocacy on behalf of the rare disease community.

"People living with rare diseases and the families who support them deserve access to information they can trust, and clinicians need reliable resources they can use in real time," said Pamela Gavin, MBA, Chief Executive Officer of NORD.

"Rare disease is exactly the kind of problem AI should be helping to solve: a vast, fragmented literature that no single clinician can master on their own," said Travis Zack, MD, PhD, Chief Medical Officer of OpenEvidence.

"By combining the scale and synthesis capabilities of AI with review from NORD experts, we can build resources that are comprehensive, current, and trustworthy, for both the clinicians and the patients they serve."
Patients can wait years for answers, and even after diagnosis, families and clinicians alike must navigate a fast-moving and highly fragmented body of information across thousands of rare conditions.
Experts recommended by NORD will help review the clinician-facing content to support clinical accuracy, real-world relevance, and alignment with the latest rare disease research and care practices.

extraction.body: NORWELL, Mass. and MIAMI , March 12, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- The National Organization for Rare Disorders (NORD ® ) and OpenEvidence today announced a new partnership to expand access to trusted, expert-reviewed rare disease information for clinicians, patients and families. Together, NORD and OpenEvidence will help build and scale a growing library of rare disease summaries in both clinician-focused and patient-friendly formats, combining AI-powered synthesis of the biomedical literature with expert review from specialists recommended by NORD, including experts from the NORD ® Rare Disease Centers of Excellence Network. The collaboration is designed to make high-quality rare disease information easier to find, easier to understand, and easier to keep current for the communities that need it most. For the more than 30 million Americans and more than 300 million people worldwide living with a rare disease, the path to diagnosis and care is often long, complex and isolating. Patients can wait years for answers, and even after diagnosis, families and clinicians alike must navigate a fast-moving and highly fragmented body of information across thousands of rare conditions. This partnership aims to help close that gap by expanding the availability of expertly reviewed content and updating it on an ongoing basis as evidence evolves. OpenEvidence plans to launch a library of more than 3,000 rare disease summaries, updated monthly through its editorial system. Experts recommended by NORD will help review the clinician-facing content to support clinical accuracy, real-world relevance, and alignment with the latest rare disease research and care practices. NORD will also support the development of patient-friendly versions designed to make complex medical information more accessible to patients, caregivers, and families. These resources will help extend the reach of trusted rare disease education beyond the point of care and support more informed conversations throughout the diagnostic and treatment journey. "People living with rare diseases and the families who support them deserve access to information they can trust, and clinicians need reliable resources they can use in real time," said Pamela Gavin, MBA, Chief Executive Officer of NORD. "Our partnership with OpenEvidence will help bring more expert-reviewed rare disease information into the world in formats designed for both clinical care and patient understanding. It is an important step toward connecting emerging knowledge with informed care and empowered patients." The rare disease pages are integrated directly into the OpenEvidence platform, where they surface automatically when clinically relevant and synthesize the latest research into a clear, practical format for clinicians. Patient-friendly versions will be disseminated through NORD Rare Disease Database to help reach patients, caregivers and families worldwide. By combining advanced AI capabilities with human expert review, the collaboration is intended to increase both scale and quality: more conditions covered, more frequently updated, and more accessible to the clinicians and families navigating rare disease every day. "Rare disease is exactly the kind of problem AI should be helping to solve: a vast, fragmented literature that no single clinician can master on their own," said Travis Zack, MD, PhD, Chief Medical Officer of OpenEvidence. "By combining the scale and synthesis capabilities of AI with review from NORD experts, we can build resources that are comprehensive, current, and trustworthy, for both the clinicians and the patients they serve." Together, NORD and OpenEvidence aim to strengthen the connection between clinical knowledge and patient education, helping clinicians recognize rare conditions sooner, supporting more informed care decisions and giving patients and families better access to understandable, up-to-date information throughout their journey. In partnership with more than 350 disease-specific member patient organizations and 46 NORD Rare Disease Centers of Excellence, NORD advances care, research, education and advocacy on behalf of the rare disease community. Understanding the Role of AI-Driven Rare Disease Patient Finder Technology An AI-driven rare disease patient finder is a sophisticated platform that utilizes artificial intelligence algorithms to identify and connect patients with rare diseases to relevant clinical trials, research studies, and tailored treatments. It processes a variety of data types, including medical records, genetic profiles, and real-world health information, to accurately pinpoint suitable patients. By enhancing the efficiency of patient identification, this technology helps speed up research efforts, boosts clinical trial enrollment, and supports the development of more targeted therapies for rare diseases. Digital Health and Telemedicine as Catalysts in Market Expansion The growing acceptance of digital health and telemedicine is a key factor propelling the expansion of the AI-driven rare disease patient finder market. Digital health encompasses the use of technology, software, and electronic tools to monitor, manage, and improve health outcomes. Telemedicine involves delivering healthcare remotely through telecommunications technology like video calls, mobile applications, and online platforms. Both patients and healthcare providers increasingly favor these solutions for their convenience, time efficiency, and accessibility. AI-driven rare disease patient finders complement digital health and telemedicine by accurately identifying patients, which enables remote monitoring, timely virtual consultations, and personalized treatment plans. For example, the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) reported in November 2025 that member countries have made significant progress in expanding access to EHRs. In 2024, the average availability of online digital health services reached 82%, up from 79% in 2023 among countries with comparable data. This growing adoption of digital health infrastructure is a major driver of the AI patient finder market’s growth. extraction.body: NORWELL, Mass. and MIAMI , March 12, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- The National Organization for Rare Disorders (NORD ® ) and OpenEvidence today announced a new partnership to expand access to trusted, expert-reviewed rare disease information for clinicians, patients and families. Together, NORD and OpenEvidence will help build and scale a growing library of rare disease summaries in both clinician-focused and patient-friendly formats, combining AI-powered synthesis of the biomedical literature with expert review from specialists recommended by NORD, including experts from the NORD ® Rare Disease Centers of Excellence Network. The collaboration is designed to make high-quality rare disease information easier to find, easier to understand, and easier to keep current for the communities that need it most. For the more than 30 million Americans and more than 300 million people worldwide living with a rare disease, the path to diagnosis and care is often long, complex and isolating. Patients can wait years for answers, and even after diagnosis, families and clinicians alike must navigate a fast-moving and highly fragmented body of information across thousands of rare conditions. This partnership aims to help close that gap by expanding the availability of expertly reviewed content and updating it on an ongoing basis as evidence evolves. OpenEvidence plans to launch a library of more than 3,000 rare disease summaries, updated monthly through its editorial system. Experts recommended by NORD will help review the clinician-facing content to support clinical accuracy, real-world relevance, and alignment with the latest rare disease research and care practices. NORD will also support the development of patient-friendly versions designed to make complex medical information more accessible to patients, caregivers, and families. These resources will help extend the reach of trusted rare disease education beyond the point of care and support more informed conversations throughout the diagnostic and treatment journey. "People living with rare diseases and the families who support them deserve access to information they can trust, and clinicians need reliable resources they can use in real time," said Pamela Gavin, MBA, Chief Executive Officer of NORD. "Our partnership with OpenEvidence will help bring more expert-reviewed rare disease information into the world in formats designed for both clinical care and patient understanding. It is an important step toward connecting emerging knowledge with informed care and empowered patients." The rare disease pages are integrated directly into the OpenEvidence platform, where they surface automatically when clinically relevant and synthesize the latest research into a clear, practical format for clinicians. Patient-friendly versions will be disseminated through NORD Rare Disease Database to help reach patients, caregivers and families worldwide. By combining advanced AI capabilities with human expert review, the collaboration is intended to increase both scale and quality: more conditions covered, more frequently updated, and more accessible to the clinicians and families navigating rare disease every day. "Rare disease is exactly the kind of problem AI should be helping to solve: a vast, fragmented literature that no single clinician can master on their own," said Travis Zack, MD, PhD, Chief Medical Officer of OpenEvidence. "By combining the scale and synthesis capabilities of AI with review from NORD experts, we can build resources that are comprehensive, current, and trustworthy, for both the clinicians and the patients they serve." Together, NORD and OpenEvidence aim to strengthen the connection between clinical knowledge and patient education, helping clinicians recognize rare conditions sooner, supporting more informed care decisions and giving patients and families better access to understandable, up-to-date information throughout their journey. AUSTIN, Texas & BARCELONA, Spain, November 03, 2026 --( BUSINESS WIRE )-- Fal.Con Europe 2026-- CrowdStrike (NASDAQ: CRWD) today announced it has signed a definitive agreement to acquire Dreadnode , a leader in Automated AI Security Testing. Dreadnode will extend the Falcon platform to continuously test every AI model, application, and agent for security weaknesses before deployment.

"Enterprises are deploying AI faster than they can prove it is secure. A model can be jailbroken, an agent can be manipulated, and most organizations have no way to find those flaws until the AI is already in production," said George Kurtz, CEO and founder of CrowdStrike. "With Dreadnode, CrowdStrike will give every enterprise the power to trust AI and deploy faster, with confidence."
Building AI Trust: Securing the AI Enterprises Build and Deploy

AI has broken the security testing model, which has traditionally been applied against code that behaves the same way every time. AI models and agents are probabilistic, can be jailbroken or manipulated through prompt injection, and fail in ways conventional testing was not designed to catch. Those weaknesses live inside the model and the agent's reasoning loop, the layer conventional testing never reaches. Identifying and fixing AI weaknesses needs to happen at the speed AI is being deployed.

With this acquisition, Dreadnode will extend the Falcon platform into the layer where enterprises build and test AI, delivering Automated AI Security Testing capabilities that extend CrowdStrike's leadership in the AI Detection and Response (AIDR) category. A utomated AI Security Testing will be generally available in Q4 FY27.
Dreadnode: Automated AI Security Testing on the Falcon Platform
With Dreadnode, CrowdStrike will deliver Automated AI Security Testing on the Falcon platform:

Automated AI Security Testing : Describe what to test in plain language. Dreadnode runs more than 100 known AI attack strategies, including jailbreaks, prompt injection, and multi-turn and agent-specific attacks, against the models, agent reasoning loops, applications, and MCP servers that power enterprise AI.

Findings, Remediation, and Framework Mapping : Dreadnode ranks findings by severity, maps them to OWASP Top 10 for LLMs, OWASP Agentic Security (ASI01-ASI10), MITRE ATLAS, and NIST AI RMF, and delivers exportable reports so teams can make go/no-go decisions before deployment.
Model and Component Scanning : Dreadnode scans AI models, model repositories, and components for vulnerabilities before they reach production.
Human-in-the-Loop Review : Operators reclassify findings, adjust severity, and document their reasoning, with dashboard metrics recomputing automatically.

Falcon Guardian and SafeMind Integration : Dreadnode findings will feed Falcon Guardian as policy recommendations, so a weakness found in testing strengthens runtime protection, and Dreadnode testing data will strengthen CrowdStrike's SafeMind models.
Expanding CrowdStrike's Cyber Superintelligence Lab

The Dreadnode team will join CrowdStrike's Cyber Superintelligence Lab, deepening the company's bench of AI security researchers. Dreadnode's technology will also sharpen how SafeMind measures the security and cyber capabilities of frontier models, advancing CrowdStrike's research into securing AI systems.

"AI fails in ways traditional testing was never designed to catch, and the people best equipped to find those failures think like attackers. We founded Dreadnode to expose those weaknesses before AI reaches production," said Brad Palm, CEO of Dreadnode. "As part of CrowdStrike, we will bring Automated AI Security Testing to every enterprise, helping teams confidently find and fix weaknesses."

The purchase price is contemplated to be paid predominantly in cash and includes a portion to be delivered in the form of stock subject to vesting conditions. The proposed acquisition is expected to close during CrowdStrike's fourth quarter of FY27, subject to customary closing conditions.

Purpose-built in the cloud with a single lightweight-agent architecture, the Falcon platform delivers rapid and scalable deployment, superior protection and performance, reduced complexity, and immediate time-to-value.

extraction.body: Cybersecurity giant CrowdStrike is buying two AI security companies that expand its products to more broadly monitor, test, and cover AI models and agents, as companies across industries start rolling out AI agents and models wholesale. CrowdStrike said it will buy Fiddler AI , which makes observability software for monitoring AI agents inside enterprises, and Dreadnode , which helps companies automate security testing specifically aimed at detecting flaws in AI models, apps, and agents before they are set live. The company is paying around $400 million for Fiddler AI, and about $95 million for Dreadnode, according to The Wall Street Journal . The deals are happening at a time of significant upheaval in the cybersecurity space, especially as companies’ policies and processes lag behind AI adoption within their walls. Teams and individual employees alike are experimenting with AI tools, automating workflows, vibe-coding custom apps, and deploying armies of AI agents to do their bidding, which is understandably causing headaches for security teams. CrowdStrike, whose products are used widely across enterprises and governments, is clearly trying to leverage its already significant heft and presence to capture a share of this quickly burgeoning market . It’s not alone, of course, as we’ve already seen several startups and cybersecurity vendors raising dozens of millions in funding to solve issues for companies, though most of these approaches are essentially based on the conviction that existing security software isn’t enough to monitor and control AI tools, connectors, or usage. The company has itself been building detection and response controls , dubbed Falcon Guardian, to help companies see and understand what agents are doing on their devices, and these acquisitions seem to further flesh out its offerings. Fiddler AI is going to be part of CrowdStrike’s Falcon platform as Falcon Observe, where it’ll ostensibly help the company’s clients evaluate agents before they’re deployed, understand their actions, and monitor what they do, and feed that information as telemetry into the broader platform. Dreadnode, meanwhile, will be integrated into the Falcon Guardian product , to which the startup’s software will feed its testing results as security policy recommendations. Founded in 2018, Fiddler AI has raised a total of about $99 million to date, according to PitchBook. Dreadnode, founded in 2023, has raised $14 million so far. coreStoryFacts.text: AUSTIN, Texas & BARCELONA, Spain, November 03, 2026 --( BUSINESS WIRE )-- Fal.Con Europe 2026-- CrowdStrike (NASDAQ: CRWD) today announced it has signed a definitive agreement to acquire Dreadnode , a leader in Automated AI Security Testing.
Dreadnode will extend the Falcon platform to continuously test every AI model, application, and agent for security weaknesses before deployment.
"AI fails in ways traditional testing was never designed to catch, and the people best equipped to find those failures think like attackers.
We founded Dreadnode to expose those weaknesses before AI reaches production," said Brad Palm, CEO of Dreadnode.

Dreadnode runs more than 100 known AI attack strategies, including jailbreaks, prompt injection, and multi-turn and agent-specific attacks, against the models, agent reasoning loops, applications, and MCP servers that power enterprise AI.
"Enterprises are deploying AI faster than they can prove it is secure.
"With Dreadnode, CrowdStrike will give every enterprise the power to trust AI and deploy faster, with confidence."
Yahoo Finance is not a broker-dealer or investment adviser and does not offer securities or cryptocurrencies for sale or facilitate trading.
The Dreadnode team will join CrowdStrike's Cyber Superintelligence Lab, deepening the company's bench of AI security researchers.
Dreadnode's technology will also sharpen how SafeMind measures the security and cyber capabilities of frontier models, advancing CrowdStrike's research into securing AI systems.

Powered by the CrowdStrike Security Cloud and world-class AI, the CrowdStrike Falcon® platform leverages real-time indicators of attack, threat intelligence, evolving adversary tradecraft, and enriched telemetry from across the enterprise to deliver hyper-accurate detections, automated protection and remediation, elite threat hunting, and prioritized observability of vulnerabilities.
You should not place undue reliance on these forward-looking statements, as actual outcomes and results may differ materially from those contemplated as a result of risks and uncertainties.

Falcon Guardian and SafeMind Integration : Dreadnode findings will feed Falcon Guardian as policy recommendations, so a weakness found in testing strengthens runtime protection, and Dreadnode testing data will strengthen CrowdStrike's SafeMind models.

Dreadnode will extend the Falcon platform with automated testing of AI models, applications, and agents to build AI trust – finding and fixing weaknesses before they reach production AUSTIN, Texas & BARCELONA, Spain, November 03, 2026 --( BUSINESS WIRE )-- Fal.Con Europe 2026-- CrowdStrike (NASDAQ: CRWD) today announced it has signed a definitive agreement to acquire Dreadnode , a leader in Automated AI Security Testing. Dreadnode will extend the Falcon platform to continuously test every AI model, application, and agent for security weaknesses before deployment. "Enterprises are deploying AI faster than they can prove it is secure. A model can be jailbroken, an agent can be manipulated, and most organizations have no way to find those flaws until the AI is already in production," said George Kurtz, CEO and founder of CrowdStrike. "With Dreadnode, CrowdStrike will give every enterprise the power to trust AI and deploy faster, with confidence." Building AI Trust: Securing the AI Enterprises Build and Deploy AI has broken the security testing model, which has traditionally been applied against code that behaves the same way every time. AI models and agents are probabilistic, can be jailbroken or manipulated through prompt injection, and fail in ways conventional testing was not designed to catch. Those weaknesses live inside the model and the agent's reasoning loop, the layer conventional testing never reaches. Identifying and fixing AI weaknesses needs to happen at the speed AI is being deployed. With this acquisition, Dreadnode will extend the Falcon platform into the layer where enterprises build and test AI, delivering Automated AI Security Testing capabilities that extend CrowdStrike's leadership in the AI Detection and Response (AIDR) category. A utomated AI Security Testing will be generally available in Q4 FY27. Dreadnode: Automated AI Security Testing on the Falcon Platform With Dreadnode, CrowdStrike will deliver Automated AI Security Testing on the Falcon platform: Automated AI Security Testing : Describe what to test in plain language. Dreadnode runs more than 100 known AI attack strategies, including jailbreaks, prompt injection, and multi-turn and agent-specific attacks, against the models, agent reasoning loops, applications, and MCP servers that power enterprise AI. Findings, Remediation, and Framework Mapping : Dreadnode ranks findings by severity, maps them to OWASP Top 10 for LLMs, OWASP Agentic Security (ASI01-ASI10), MITRE ATLAS, and NIST AI RMF, and delivers exportable reports so teams can make go/no-go decisions before deployment. Model and Component Scanning : Dreadnode scans AI models, model repositories, and components for vulnerabilities before they reach production. Human-in-the-Loop Review : Operators reclassify findings, adjust severity, and document their reasoning, with dashboard metrics recomputing automatically. Falcon Guardian and SafeMind Integration : Dreadnode findings will feed Falcon Guardian as policy recommendations, so a weakness found in testing strengthens runtime protection, and Dreadnode testing data will strengthen CrowdStrike's SafeMind models. Expanding CrowdStrike's Cyber Superintelligence Lab The Dreadnode team will join CrowdStrike's Cyber Superintelligence Lab, deepening the company's bench of AI security researchers. Dreadnode's technology will also sharpen how SafeMind measures the security and cyber capabilities of frontier models, advancing CrowdStrike's research into securing AI systems. "AI fails in ways traditional testing was never designed to catch, and the people best equipped to find those failures think like attackers. We founded Dreadnode to expose those weaknesses before AI reaches production," said Brad Palm, CEO of Dreadnode. "As part of CrowdStrike, we will bring Automated AI Security Testing to every enterprise, helping teams confidently find and fix weaknesses." AUSTIN, Texas & BARCELONA, Spain, November 03, 2026 --( BUSINESS WIRE )-- Fal.Con Europe 2026-- CrowdStrike (NASDAQ: CRWD) today announced it has signed a definitive agreement to acquire Dreadnode , a leader in Automated AI Security Testing. Dreadnode will extend the Falcon platform to continuously test every AI model, application, and agent for security weaknesses before deployment.

"Enterprises are deploying AI faster than they can prove it is secure. A model can be jailbroken, an agent can be manipulated, and most organizations have no way to find those flaws until the AI is already in production," said George Kurtz, CEO and founder of CrowdStrike. "With Dreadnode, CrowdStrike will give every enterprise the power to trust AI and deploy faster, with confidence."
Building AI Trust: Securing the AI Enterprises Build and Deploy

AI has broken the security testing model, which has traditionally been applied against code that behaves the same way every time. AI models and agents are probabilistic, can be jailbroken or manipulated through prompt injection, and fail in ways conventional testing was not designed to catch. Those weaknesses live inside the model and the agent's reasoning loop, the layer conventional testing never reaches. Identifying and fixing AI weaknesses needs to happen at the speed AI is being deployed.

With this acquisition, Dreadnode will extend the Falcon platform into the layer where enterprises build and test AI, delivering Automated AI Security Testing capabilities that extend CrowdStrike's leadership in the AI Detection and Response (AIDR) category. A utomated AI Security Testing will be generally available in Q4 FY27.
Dreadnode: Automated AI Security Testing on the Falcon Platform
With Dreadnode, CrowdStrike will deliver Automated AI Security Testing on the Falcon platform:

Automated AI Security Testing : Describe what to test in plain language. Dreadnode runs more than 100 known AI attack strategies, including jailbreaks, prompt injection, and multi-turn and agent-specific attacks, against the models, agent reasoning loops, applications, and MCP servers that power enterprise AI.

Findings, Remediation, and Framework Mapping : Dreadnode ranks findings by severity, maps them to OWASP Top 10 for LLMs, OWASP Agentic Security (ASI01-ASI10), MITRE ATLAS, and NIST AI RMF, and delivers exportable reports so teams can make go/no-go decisions before deployment.
Model and Component Scanning : Dreadnode scans AI models, model repositories, and components for vulnerabilities before they reach production.
Human-in-the-Loop Review : Operators reclassify findings, adjust severity, and document their reasoning, with dashboard metrics recomputing automatically.

Falcon Guardian and SafeMind Integration : Dreadnode findings will feed Falcon Guardian as policy recommendations, so a weakness found in testing strengthens runtime protection, and Dreadnode testing data will strengthen CrowdStrike's SafeMind models.
Expanding CrowdStrike's Cyber Superintelligence Lab

The Dreadnode team will join CrowdStrike's Cyber Superintelligence Lab, deepening the company's bench of AI security researchers. Dreadnode's technology will also sharpen how SafeMind measures the security and cyber capabilities of frontier models, advancing CrowdStrike's research into securing AI systems.

"AI fails in ways traditional testing was never designed to catch, and the people best equipped to find those failures think like attackers. We founded Dreadnode to expose those weaknesses before AI reaches production," said Brad Palm, CEO of Dreadnode. "As part of CrowdStrike, we will bring Automated AI Security Testing to every enterprise, helping teams confidently find and fix weaknesses."

sources.title: CrowdStrike to shell out nearly $500M for 2 AI security startups as the market for securing agents takes off
passages: Fiddler AI is going to be part of CrowdStrike’s Falcon platform as Falcon Observe, where it’ll ostensibly help the company’s clients evaluate agents before they’re deployed, understand their actions, and monitor what they do, and feed that information as telemetry into the broader platform.

Cybersecurity giant CrowdStrike is buying two AI security companies that expand its products to more broadly monitor, test, and cover AI models and agents, as companies across industries start rolling out AI agents and models wholesale.

CrowdStrike, whose products are used widely across enterprises and governments, is clearly trying to leverage its already significant heft and presence to capture a share of this quickly burgeoning market .

It’s not alone, of course, as we’ve already seen several startups and cybersecurity vendors raising dozens of millions in funding to solve issues for companies, though most of these approaches are essentially based on the conviction that existing security software isn’t enough to monitor and control AI tools, connectors, or usage.

Teams and individual employees alike are experimenting with AI tools, automating workflows, vibe-coding custom apps, and deploying armies of AI agents to do their bidding, which is understandably causing headaches for security teams.

extraction.body: Cybersecurity giant CrowdStrike is buying two AI security companies that expand its products to more broadly monitor, test, and cover AI models and agents, as companies across industries start rolling out AI agents and models wholesale. CrowdStrike said it will buy Fiddler AI , which makes observability software for monitoring AI agents inside enterprises, and Dreadnode , which helps companies automate security testing specifically aimed at detecting flaws in AI models, apps, and agents before they are set live. The company is paying around $400 million for Fiddler AI, and about $95 million for Dreadnode, according to The Wall Street Journal . The deals are happening at a time of significant upheaval in the cybersecurity space, especially as companies’ policies and processes lag behind AI adoption within their walls. Teams and individual employees alike are experimenting with AI tools, automating workflows, vibe-coding custom apps, and deploying armies of AI agents to do their bidding, which is understandably causing headaches for security teams. CrowdStrike, whose products are used widely across enterprises and governments, is clearly trying to leverage its already significant heft and presence to capture a share of this quickly burgeoning market . It’s not alone, of course, as we’ve already seen several startups and cybersecurity vendors raising dozens of millions in funding to solve issues for companies, though most of these approaches are essentially based on the conviction that existing security software isn’t enough to monitor and control AI tools, connectors, or usage. The company has itself been building detection and response controls , dubbed Falcon Guardian, to help companies see and understand what agents are doing on their devices, and these acquisitions seem to further flesh out its offerings. Fiddler AI is going to be part of CrowdStrike’s Falcon platform as Falcon Observe, where it’ll ostensibly help the company’s clients evaluate agents before they’re deployed, understand their actions, and monitor what they do, and feed that information as telemetry into the broader platform. Dreadnode, meanwhile, will be integrated into the Falcon Guardian product , to which the startup’s software will feed its testing results as security policy recommendations. Founded in 2018, Fiddler AI has raised a total of about $99 million to date, according to PitchBook. Dreadnode, founded in 2023, has raised $14 million so far. extraction.body: Crypto giant Binance says North Korean hackers used fake social media profiles and the lure of a potential job offer as part of a months-long scheme aimed at tricking an employee into downloading malicious software onto their laptop. Researchers have repeatedly warned about long-running social engineering attacks that can go on for months. This latest attack allowed the hackers to patiently worm their way into Binance's systems to steal a record $6.3 billion in crypto last week, the company has now confirmed. The hack, disclosed in an updated statement posted on X on Tuesday, prompted the world's largest crypto exchange to suspend customer withdrawals across its network. The FBI and blockchain investigators have blamed North Korea for the heist. The country has been long accused of carrying out massive cryptocurrency thefts in recent years to fund its internationally sanctioned nuclear weapons program. In its latest statement, Binance said that North Korean hackers, posing as recruiters hiring for a job, contacted a software engineer who works on wallets at the company. Following two interviews with the purported company, the engineer was instructed to download an apparent coding assignment as part of the interview process. When opened, the assignment contained malicious code that compromised the engineer's work-issued laptop. Binance said its security tools did not detect the malware. That foothold in Binance's network allowed the hackers to access an internal tool capable of taking over the work computers of two other engineers on the wallet team. One of those engineers had unwittingly downloaded a tampered app containing password-stealing malware months earlier after searching for the software in search engine results. While Binance replaced that compromised engineer's laptop, the hackers used the engineer's stolen credentials to break into the computer of a third engineer, whose job allowed them access to systems capable of controlling billions of dollars in crypto. Binance said the attack "should not have happened," and that it had improved its network security following the theft. The hack underscores an ongoing tactic in the North Korean regime's repertoire of attacks targeting the crypto industry and high-net worth individuals. Researchers have warned for years that North Korean hackers pose as venture capitalists, investors, and recruiters using dossiers of stolen American identities to trick employees into granting access to their systems. These attacks are widely known across the crypto industry and have been the subject of repeated warnings from the U.S. government and cybersecurity giants in recent years. Some half of all intrusions at U.S. tech companies last year were attributed to North Koreans posing as remote IT workers and fake recruiters. By Binance's own account, the company faced at least 57 suspected attacks from North Korea, which it said reflect the "persistent threat posed by state-sponsored actors targeting the cryptocurrency industry." But how the hackers were able to convince the engineer into downloading malware given the highly publicized threat, and bypass security weaknesses in Binance's own network, will likely be the focus of investigators' attention. While the case exposes how North Korean hackers use social engineering, such as offers of employment, to trick employees into granting access to their systems, it's ultimately the responsibility of the company to ensure its systems cannot run unauthorized or untrusted software that could cause a compromise. A Binance spokesperson referred to the company's public statement but declined to answer TechCrunch's questions on the record about the incident. Those questions included how Binance prevents unauthorized or malicious code from running on its employees' laptops, if at all, and whether any third parties had performed cybersecurity audits of Binance's network prior to the hack. The company said it would bring in cybersecurity experts to review the incident and has put new security measures in place to prevent a repeat incident. The heist remains the largest theft of crypto in history. Updated to remove name of Binance spokesperson in thirteenth paragraph.

passages: A $10,000 investment in NVIDIA ( NASDAQ:NVDA ) made five years ago, on November 3, 2021, has grown to approximately $76,300 by November 2, 2026.
In comparison, the same amount invested in Bitcoin (CRYPTO:BTC) has only increased to about $12,200.
This dramatic difference highlights why the Bitcoin vs.
Nvidia competition isn't even close, despite both facing some tough times recently.
Nvidia has clearly outperformed Bitcoin over the past five years.
Over a three-year period, Bitcoin posted strong annual growth of about 30.2%, but Nvidia still outperformed at 65.1% per year.
Over the last year, Bitcoin holders lost far more value than those who invested in Nvidia.
Nvidia's recovery from its 2022 crash was powered by $215.9 billion in fiscal 2026 revenue, while Bitcoin has no earnings to speak of and depends entirely on market demand.
Both Bitcoin and Nvidia fell sharply early in the five-year timeframe.
Bitcoin fell dramatically from peak to trough by 76.6%, reaching its lowest point on November 21, 2022.
Nvidia, while also affected, fell less, down 66.4% from its November 29, 2021 close to its October 14, 2022 close.
When tech stocks face volatility, Bitcoin tends to decline as well, as seen recently following the Binance hack in late October.
Although Bitcoin showed a strong percentage increase over three years because of its lower starting price, its five-year performance is lackluster compared to Nvidia.
Both assets still carry risks; if Nvidia's future earnings reports fall short of expectations, it could create a downward trend for both Nvidia and Bitcoin.
